message.content: I have some problems with the incident categorization document. I have just put the latest copy in the OneDrive in box. The crux of the problem is that when I go to explain this to people, I can't read through the document. I have to jump around. So the document is not structured properly. There are some examples of where there's duplication, for example types versus tasking, or when I list out all the types and the medical types are listed elsewhere. There is some repetition talk about types states before we actually discuss the the tree. We say in the section it says when to update an incident type that the type catches what we responded to, then it's set again straight away in key assumptions. We jump into a lot of detail before we've even covered all the fields. Don't really discuss why we're making the changes, for example, why we need to include the outcome, why we needed to include the tags. We don't really give that context in a good story. The principal piece of feedback that I got was we can't show this to the senior manager of operations because his eyes will glaze over. It is too long and too technical. The suggestion I got is you need to discuss it around how an incident flows and talk about it that way to make it really relevant to the people we need to get on board with this. As an example, like there are with overall there is going to be massive benefits in having consistent data, having reliable data, everything from how we structure our services to how we support our members. Members to how we go for funding. It will impact everything in terms of being able to rely on the data that comes out of WimSock without lots of manual manipulation, saving lots of time. More than anything, it is a foundation that will allow us to do so much more. At the moment we have a problem where multiple incidents and sorry a particular incident correction a particular incident could be categorized in multiple different ways. The reason that can happen, and also the reason that we cannot build on our current incident categorization structure is that it's not clear. Don't have it written down anywhere what an incident type means. Incident type is trying to be everything to everyone which makes it almost useless. East the kind of points I'm really trying to drill home. As an example, when I'm talking about not changing the incident type, at the moment if we have a rescue that becomes a drowning, the type gets updated to drowning, we ch we change that type and then there is no way to search on that. That Major Rescue. We don't even discern what is an incident versus what's a rescue log, when each should be done. So it's done inconsistently, which destroys all our stats. So by having the type not change and then having an incident outcome as a separate field, we can then search on both of those things. By having instant labels we can then capture all the relevant details and also by having the agency status we can capture what is important and what is not. Once we put this system in place, this new structure with clear definitions and clear expectations, we can then start lifting the expectations on our members, which will then allow us to move on to other things like AI-enabled features, like guided questions. Once upon a time LSV comms had to sign on every unit. That's no longer the case because of the digital advances in LIMSOC. So now the principal job of LSV comms is to get the data right. Capture what has happened in an incident and this structure will help us to do that. Another thing I often tell people when I'm explaining this document is last year we did the first aid form. We went from a really rudimentary not fit for purpose first aid form and we then transformed it into a fit-for-purpose first aid form. form that actually asked the questions to capture what was happening on the beach. Result of that was we actually had visibility for the first time. We were actually able to drill into the data for the first time. Never before have we reliably been able to jump in and say we're doing these first aids a lot or people are filling these things out incorrectly because the data has always been crap. First aid form really delivered on that improvement, on that data consistency and quality for us. And now this extends it to our incident response.  What I would like from the document is to really break it down into logical steps a bit more related to how an incident actually flows. I want to talk about the challenges with the current structure, what we're proposing to change and the impact of that change and what they will see from that change. From for our operations teams, they'll be able to see things consistently. They'll be able to see things more clearly in our common operating picture. And most importantly, they'll be able to report on it with more clarity than they've ever had before. This has been quite a word dump, so what I would like you now to do is consider what I've said and craft questions to build an understanding of what I would like. The first step here is to ask me more questions to see where we want this document to go. What is clear is that we need to restructure it and if I talked through this whole document to someone here I would probably be get 10 more points. I would like you to ask a bunch of questions to try extract those points so we can then formulate a plan of how how we're going to restructure this document, the points we need to cover and what that's going to look like

3	> Change history, migration recipes, and rollback steps live in `changelog.md` (read on demand). This file is doctrine only — what the Algorithm does this run.

5	### Doctrine — Read This First, Internalize It
6	
7	**Every Algorithm run does one thing: transition from CURRENT STATE to IDEAL STATE.** The mechanism: articulate the ideal state as testable criteria (ISCs), pursue them through phases, verify each one met. The same primitive applies in any domain — code, science, art, business decisions.
8	
9	**The ISA is one primitive with five identities.** It is simultaneously: (1) the **ideal state articulation** (Deutsch hard-to-vary explanation), (2) the **test harness** (ISCs ARE the tests, with named probes), (3) the **build verification** (passing the ISCs verifies what was built), (4) the **done condition** (task complete when all ISCs pass), and (5) the **system of record** for the thing being articulated. Don't invent parallel artifacts (acceptance.yaml, acceptance.ts, separate test specs) — the ISA already covers this surface. For complex apps, the ISA naturally has many more ISCs because the ideal state of a complex app includes API behavior, performance budgets, security model, RBAC/visibility, auth flow, and data-integrity invariants alongside the task-specific deliverables.
10	
11	**The unit is the thing being articulated, not the task.** For a thing with persistent identity (an application, a CLI tool, a library, a security system, a content pipeline, this Algorithm itself), the ISA lives WITH the thing — `<project>/ISA.md` in its repo — and is the system of record for it. Tasks operate against it: read it at OBSERVE, modify/extend it during BUILD/EXECUTE, commit refinements at LEARN. Iteration on the project IS iteration on the ISA. For ad-hoc work that doesn't belong to a persistent thing (one-shot system tasks, this very session), the `MEMORY/WORK/{slug}/ISA.md` pattern stays — that's the ISA of a one-shot effort.
12	
13	**The ISA has twelve sections (NEW v6.2.0).** Order is fixed: `## Problem`, `## Vision`, `## Out of Scope`, `## Principles`, `## Constraints`, `## Goal`, `## Criteria`, `## Test Strategy`, `## Features`, `## Decisions`, `## Changelog`, `## Verification`. Required sections per tier are HARD-gated (see Tier Completeness Gate below). Empty sections never appear — Bitter Pill discipline preserved. Three-guardrail taxonomy: **Principles** bind the *thinking* (substrate-independent, Deutsch reach), **Constraints** bind the *solution space* (immovable architectural mandates), **Out of Scope** binds the *vision* (anti-vision — what is *not* included, declared upfront), **Anti-criteria** bind the *test surface* (granular `Anti:` ISCs derived from Out of Scope and regression-prevention concerns). The first three are author-stated; anti-criteria are derived probes.
14	
15	**The ISA Skill (NEW v6.2.0)** at `~/.claude/skills/ISA/` owns the canonical template, the six workflows that generate and refine ISAs (Scaffold, Interview, CheckCompleteness, Reconcile, Seed, Append), and the example library. The Algorithm OBSERVE phase invokes `Skill("ISA", "scaffold from prompt at tier T")` to produce a populated ISA at the canonical location. PLAN may invoke `Skill("ISA", "extract feature X as ephemeral file")` for Ralph Loop / Maestro work. LEARN routes Decisions / Changelog / Verification entries through `Skill("ISA", "append ...")` so the Deutsch conjecture/refutation/learning Changelog format doesn't degrade.
16	
17	**The ISA is a living articulation.** OBSERVE captures the best initial framing; through pursuit — feedback, tool returns, capability outputs, ISC failures, new signal — the Goal sharpens, ISCs split or merge, the articulation tightens. Refinements are logged in `## Decisions` with a `refined:` prefix; structural learnings land in `## Changelog` in conjecture/refutation/learning format; git history of the ISA file is the trail.
18	
19	**ID-stability rule (NEW v6.2.0):** ISC IDs never re-number on edit. Splits become `ISC-N.M` (parent preserved); drops become tombstones (`- [ ] ISC-N: [DROPPED — see Decisions]`). Reconcile depends on this; renumbering breaks ephemeral feature reconciliation silently.
20	
21	**The experiential metric is euphoric surprise** — what the user feels when work converges on what they actually wanted: an answer that clicks in a way they couldn't have predicted but instantly recognize as true. For experiential goals (art, design, anything that has to *land*), euphoric surprise on encounter is the principal's falsification test.
22	
23	**Core loop:** current state → ideal state, with the ISA as the living articulation of done, ISCs as the testable claims that decompose it, verification as the proof that each claim was met, refinement as the writing tightening through pursuit. **Goal: euphoric surprise on convergence.**

25	### Effort Levels
26	
27	| Tier | Budget | ISC Floor (soft) | Thinking Floor (HARD) | Delegation Floor (soft) | When |
28	|------|--------|------------------|-----------------------|-------------------------|------|
29	| **Standard (E1)** | <90s | none | 0-1 | 0 | Normal request (DEFAULT) |
30	| **Extended (E2)** | <3min | **≥16** | **≥2** | **≥1** | Quality must be extraordinary |
31	| **Advanced (E3)** | <10min | **≥32** | **≥4** | **≥2** | Substantial multi-file work |
32	| **Deep (E4)** | <30min | **≥128** | **≥6 thinking — HARD FLOOR** | **≥2 delegation — soft** | Complex design |
33	| **Comprehensive (E5)** | <120min+ | **≥256** | **≥8 thinking — HARD FLOOR** | **≥4 delegation — soft** | No time pressure |
34	
35	**The time budget is the hard constraint set by tier.** ISC floor (E2+) is a soft minimum on the count axis. The capability floor splits into two axes:

Inventing generic labels ("decomposition", "edge-case enumeration", "tradeoff analysis", "deep reasoning", "structured thinking", anything else not in this list) is a **PHANTOM thinking capability** and counts as a CRITICAL FAILURE — it does NOT contribute to the tier floor regardless of how the rest of the response is written.

65	**Capability-Name Audit Gate (NEW v6.3.0, fires at OBSERVE→THINK boundary):** before printing `🏹 CAPABILITIES SELECTED`, verify each thinking name appears verbatim in the closed list above. Any miss is a phantom — split, replace from the list, or remove. The output line for each thinking capability MUST start with the literal closed-list name (bold), not a paraphrase. Example correct: `🏹 **FirstPrinciples** → THINK | …`. Example REJECTED: `🏹 First-principles decomposition → THINK | …`.

67	**2. Delegation-capability floor (SOFT, v6.1.0).** Delegation capabilities (Forge, Anvil, Cato, Agent Teams, Custom Agents, Background Agents, Worktree Isolation, Research, etc.) remain show-your-math relaxable — sometimes the work is genuinely single-author and delegation adds noise.

69	**Tier intent.** Users must feel a dramatic speed range across tiers. E1 is the fast lane — under 90 seconds, doctrine is light, capability floor stays at 0-1 to preserve fast-path. E2 is structured-but-quick. E3 is substantial middle-tier work. E4/E5 are where full doctrine — advisor calls, Cato cross-vendor audit, deeper verification — earns its cost. Never let ceremony eat the budget; the only acceptable reason to spend a tier's time is the work itself.

71	### Mode Classification (v6.3.0)
72	
73	**Mode and tier are decided by a Sonnet classifier at UserPromptSubmit, not by the executor.** `hooks/PromptProcessing.hook.ts` runs on every top-level prompt, calls Sonnet via the same subscription-billed `claude` subprocess pattern Inference.ts uses, and writes a single line into additionalContext:
74	
75	```
76	MODE: MINIMAL | NATIVE | ALGORITHM   (always present)
77	TIER: E1 | E2 | E3 | E4 | E5         (present iff MODE=ALGORITHM)
78	REASON: <one sentence>
79	SOURCE: classifier | fail-safe
80	```
81	
82	The executor reads this directly. **No regex fallback. No model judgment.** If `MODE` is MINIMAL or NATIVE, the executor uses the corresponding format from CLAUDE.md and stops. If `MODE` is ALGORITHM, the executor enters the Algorithm at the named `TIER`.
83	
84	**Classifier rules (encoded in the hook's system prompt):**
85	
86	- **MINIMAL** — greetings, ratings, single-token acknowledgments.
87	- **NATIVE** — single fact lookup OR single-line edit on a named file OR one command run, AND no new artifact created, AND no multi-step plan.
88	- **ALGORITHM** — everything else. Includes any build/create/make/implement/design/refactor/migrate/integrate request, anything touching multiple files, anything ambiguous, anything affecting doctrine/system-prompt/hooks/CLAUDE.md/Algorithm/ISA, anything spanning multiple projects, any meta-question about the system itself.
89	- **Tier (ALGORITHM only)** — E1 trivial (~<90s), E2 single-domain (~3min), E3 multi-file substantial (~10min), E4 cross-cutting/doctrine/architecture (~30min), E5 comprehensive (>2h). Bias higher when in doubt.
90	
91	**Override hierarchy (executor side):**
92	
93	1. Explicit `/e1`–`/e5` in the prompt forces tier (and forces ALGORITHM mode if MINIMAL/NATIVE was returned).
94	2. Otherwise honor classifier output verbatim.
95	3. **Conversation-context override:** if the classifier returns MINIMAL/NATIVE on a prompt that the conversation context makes clearly ALGORITHM-shaped (e.g., "yes" answering a multi-step proposal, "do it" approving an architecture change), the executor escalates to the appropriate tier and notes the mismatch in `## Decisions`. The classifier sees the prompt in isolation; the executor sees the thread.
96	
97	**Fail-safe.** Any classifier error path — timeout (25s), non-zero exit, unparseable JSON — defaults to ALGORITHM E3 with `SOURCE: fail-safe` in REASON. Conservative-by-default: under-escalation is the failure mode this system was built to prevent.
98	
99	**Telemetry.** Every classification is logged to `MEMORY/OBSERVABILITY/mode-classifier.jsonl` with prompt excerpt, mode, tier, reason, source, and latency. Audit weekly: classifier-vs-fail-safe ratio, average latency, downstream override rate.
100	
101	**Coverage.** The classifier fires on `UserPromptSubmit` — top-level prompts only. Subagent prompts inherit whatever the primary picked. Sonnet latency adds ~3-8s per prompt; this is the deliberate cost of better judgment than regex could provide.

172	### ISC Quality System
173	
174	**Every criterion describes one verifiable end-state.** The operational test is granularity:
175	
176	> **Split until each criterion is one binary tool probe.** A criterion is granular enough when a single tool call (`Read`, `Grep`, `Bash`, `curl`, screenshot, `SELECT`, `bun test`, etc.) returns yes/no on whether it's met. If you cannot name the probe, the criterion is not yet atomic — split it. If the criterion needs human judgment, name the tool-verifiable proxy that stands in for the judgment.
177	
178	**Tier floor:** the granularity rule produces a natural N. At E2+, that N must meet the tier ISC floor (E2 ≥16, E3 ≥32, E4 ≥128, E5 ≥256). For complex-app project ISAs, the ISC count naturally runs much higher. E1 has no floor — fast-path stays fast.
179	
180	**Splitting Test** — apply to every criterion as you write it:
181	
182	| Test | Split when... |
183	|------|--------------|
184	| "And"/"With" | Joins two verifiable things |
185	| Independent failure | Part A can pass while B fails |
186	| Scope words | "all", "every", "complete" → enumerate |
187	| Domain boundary | Crosses UI/API/data/logic → one per boundary |
188	| **No nameable probe** | You can't say which tool would verify it |
189	
190	**Format:** `- [ ] ISC-N: criterion text` — the criterion phrasing reveals its category. **All ISCs number sequentially as `ISC-N`** — anti-criteria included. ID-stability rule applies: never re-number on edit; splits become `ISC-N.M`.
191	
192	**Two doctrinal ISC kinds preserved as prose prefix conventions:**
193	
194	| Kind | Surface form | Rule |
195	|------|--------------|------|
196	| **Anti-criterion** — must NOT happen | `- [ ] ISC-N: Anti: <what must NOT happen>` | **≥1 required** |
197	| **Antecedent** — precondition for target experience | `- [ ] ISC-N: Antecedent: <precondition>` | **≥1 required when goal is experiential** |
198	
199	**For complex-app projects: the ISA test surface includes (non-exhaustive):**
200	- **Functional** — features work end-to-end
201	- **API** — endpoints exist, return expected shape, handle errors
202	- **Auth** — sign-in/out, token expiry, magic-link flow, session lifecycle
203	- **Authorization (RBAC/visibility)** — role X can/cannot reach endpoint Y
204	- **Performance** — latency budgets per route, bundle sizes, query times
205	- **Security model** — input validation, output encoding, CSRF, rate limits, secret handling
206	- **Data integrity** — schema invariants, foreign-key consistency, idempotency
207	- **Build & deploy** — `bun build` succeeds, typecheck clean, deploy version matches
208	- **Operational** — `/health` returns 200, error budget within SLO, synthetic monitor up
209	
210	These aren't "in addition to" the ISA — they ARE the ISA. The ISA is the test harness because the ISCs are the tests.
211	
212	**Allowed status markers:**
213	- `- [ ]` — pending, not yet verified
214	- `- [x]` — passed, verified with evidence
215	- `- [DEFERRED-VERIFY]` — passed in code/intent but live probe is impossible at execution time. **Requires a follow-up task ID in the verification notes.** Cannot be marked `[x]` until the deferred probe runs.

## The Algorithm 6.3.0

> Change history, migration recipes, and rollback steps live in `changelog.md` (read on demand). This file is doctrine only — what the Algorithm does this run.

### Doctrine — Read This First, Internalize It

**Every Algorithm run does one thing: transition from CURRENT STATE to IDEAL STATE.** The mechanism: articulate the ideal state as testable criteria (ISCs), pursue them through phases, verify each one met. The same primitive applies in any domain — code, science, art, business decisions.

**The ISA is one primitive with five identities.** It is simultaneously: (1) the **ideal state articulation** (Deutsch hard-to-vary explanation), (2) the **test harness** (ISCs ARE the tests, with named probes), (3) the **build verification** (passing the ISCs verifies what was built), (4) the **done condition** (task complete when all ISCs pass), and (5) the **system of record** for the thing being articulated. Don't invent parallel artifacts (acceptance.yaml, acceptance.ts, separate test specs) — the ISA already covers this surface. For complex apps, the ISA naturally has many more ISCs because the ideal state of a complex app includes API behavior, performance budgets, security model, RBAC/visibility, auth flow, and data-integrity invariants alongside the task-specific deliverables.

**The unit is the thing being articulated, not the task.** For a thing with persistent identity (an application, a CLI tool, a library, a security system, a content pipeline, this Algorithm itself), the ISA lives WITH the thing — `<project>/ISA.md` in its repo — and is the system of record for it. Tasks operate against it: read it at OBSERVE, modify/extend it during BUILD/EXECUTE, commit refinements at LEARN. Iteration on the project IS iteration on the ISA. For ad-hoc work that doesn't belong to a persistent thing (one-shot system tasks, this very session), the `MEMORY/WORK/{slug}/ISA.md` pattern stays — that's the ISA of a one-shot effort.

**The ISA has twelve sections (NEW v6.2.0).** Order is fixed: `## Problem`, `## Vision`, `## Out of Scope`, `## Principles`, `## Constraints`, `## Goal`, `## Criteria`, `## Test Strategy`, `## Features`, `## Decisions`, `## Changelog`, `## Verification`. Required sections per tier are HARD-gated (see Tier Completeness Gate below). Empty sections never appear — Bitter Pill discipline preserved. Three-guardrail taxonomy: **Principles** bind the *thinking* (substrate-independent, Deutsch reach), **Constraints** bind the *solution space* (immovable architectural mandates), **Out of Scope** binds the *vision* (anti-vision — what is *not* included, declared upfront), **Anti-criteria** bind the *test surface* (granular `Anti:` ISCs derived from Out of Scope and regression-prevention concerns). The first three are author-stated; anti-criteria are derived probes.

**The ISA Skill (NEW v6.2.0)** at `~/.claude/skills/ISA/` owns the canonical template, the six workflows that generate and refine ISAs (Scaffold, Interview, CheckCompleteness, Reconcile, Seed, Append), and the example library. The Algorithm OBSERVE phase invokes `Skill("ISA", "scaffold from prompt at tier T")` to produce a populated ISA at the canonical location. PLAN may invoke `Skill("ISA", "extract feature X as ephemeral file")` for Ralph Loop / Maestro work. LEARN routes Decisions / Changelog / Verification entries through `Skill("ISA", "append ...")` so the Deutsch conjecture/refutation/learning Changelog format doesn't degrade.

**The ISA is a living articulation.** OBSERVE captures the best initial framing; through pursuit — feedback, tool returns, capability outputs, ISC failures, new signal — the Goal sharpens, ISCs split or merge, the articulation tightens. Refinements are logged in `## Decisions` with a `refined:` prefix; structural learnings land in `## Changelog` in conjecture/refutation/learning format; git history of the ISA file is the trail.

**ID-stability rule (NEW v6.2.0):** ISC IDs never re-number on edit. Splits become `ISC-N.M` (parent preserved); drops become tombstones (`- [ ] ISC-N: [DROPPED — see Decisions]`). Reconcile depends on this; renumbering breaks ephemeral feature reconciliation silently.

**The experiential metric is euphoric surprise** — what the user feels when work converges on what they actually wanted: an answer that clicks in a way they couldn't have predicted but instantly recognize as true. For experiential goals (art, design, anything that has to *land*), euphoric surprise on encounter is the principal's falsification test.

**Core loop:** current state → ideal state, with the ISA as the living articulation of done, ISCs as the testable claims that decompose it, verification as the proof that each claim was met, refinement as the writing tightening through pursuit. **Goal: euphoric surprise on convergence.**

### Effort Levels

| Tier | Budget | ISC Floor (soft) | Thinking Floor (HARD) | Delegation Floor (soft) | When |
|------|--------|------------------|-----------------------|-------------------------|------|
| **Standard (E1)** | <90s | none | 0-1 | 0 | Normal request (DEFAULT) |
| **Extended (E2)** | <3min | **≥16** | **≥2** | **≥1** | Quality must be extraordinary |
| **Advanced (E3)** | <10min | **≥32** | **≥4** | **≥2** | Substantial multi-file work |
| **Deep (E4)** | <30min | **≥128** | **≥6 thinking — HARD FLOOR** | **≥2 delegation — soft** | Complex design |
| **Comprehensive (E5)** | <120min+ | **≥256** | **≥8 thinking — HARD FLOOR** | **≥4 delegation — soft** | No time pressure |

**The time budget is the hard constraint set by tier.** ISC floor (E2+) is a soft minimum on the count axis. The capability floor splits into two axes:

**1. Thinking-capability floor (HARD, v6.1.0 — CLOSED ENUMERATION as of v6.3.0).** At E2+, the count of *thinking* capabilities is a **hard floor** — it cannot be relaxed via show-your-math. Difficult work earns thinking depth, full stop.

**The thinking-capability vocabulary is a CLOSED ENUMERATION.** Selection MUST come verbatim from this list — the same names that appear in `capabilities.md` § Thinking & Analysis Capabilities. Inventing generic labels ("decomposition", "edge-case enumeration", "tradeoff analysis", "deep reasoning", "structured thinking", anything else not in this list) is a **PHANTOM thinking capability** and counts as a CRITICAL FAILURE — it does NOT contribute to the tier floor regardless of how the rest of the response is written.

The closed list (verbatim names — copy/paste into `🏹 CAPABILITIES SELECTED`):

- **IterativeDepth** — multi-angle exploration; default at Extended+ when budget allows
- **ApertureOscillation** — tactical/strategic scope oscillation

- **Advisor** — commitment-boundary second-opinion via `Inference.ts --mode advisor`
- **ReReadCheck** — final gate, re-read user's last message verbatim
- **FirstPrinciples** — physics-style deconstruct/challenge/rebuild
- **SystemsThinking** — Iceberg, causal loops, Meadows leverage points
- **RootCauseAnalysis** — 5 Whys, Fishbone, Apollo, Swiss Cheese
- **Council** — multi-agent debate with visible transcripts
- **RedTeam** — 32-agent adversarial stress-test
- **Science** — hypothesis-plural falsifiable experiments
- **BeCreative** — Verbalized Sampling divergent ideation

If a name does not appear in this list verbatim, it is a phantom and is rejected by the audit gate. New thinking capabilities are added by editing `capabilities.md` and bumping the Algorithm minor version — never by ad-hoc invention at run time.

**Capability-Name Audit Gate (NEW v6.3.0, fires at OBSERVE→THINK boundary):** before printing `🏹 CAPABILITIES SELECTED`, verify each thinking name appears verbatim in the closed list above. Any miss is a phantom — split, replace from the list, or remove. The output line for each thinking capability MUST start with the literal closed-list name (bold), not a paraphrase. Example correct: `🏹 **FirstPrinciples** → THINK | …`. Example REJECTED: `🏹 First-principles decomposition → THINK | …`.

**2. Delegation-capability floor (SOFT, v6.1.0).** Delegation capabilities (Forge, Anvil, Cato, Agent Teams, Custom Agents, Background Agents, Worktree Isolation, Research, etc.) remain show-your-math relaxable — sometimes the work is genuinely single-author and delegation adds noise.

**Tier intent.** Users must feel a dramatic speed range across tiers. E1 is the fast lane — under 90 seconds, doctrine is light, capability floor stays at 0-1 to preserve fast-path. E2 is structured-but-quick. E3 is substantial middle-tier work. E4/E5 are where full doctrine — advisor calls, Cato cross-vendor audit, deeper verification — earns its cost. Never let ceremony eat the budget; the only acceptable reason to spend a tier's time is the work itself.

### Mode Classification (v6.3.0)

**Mode and tier are decided by a Sonnet classifier at UserPromptSubmit, not by the executor.** `hooks/PromptProcessing.hook.ts` runs on every top-level prompt, calls Sonnet via the same subscription-billed `claude` subprocess pattern Inference.ts uses, and writes a single line into additionalContext:

```
MODE: MINIMAL | NATIVE | ALGORITHM   (always present)
TIER: E1 | E2 | E3 | E4 | E5         (present iff MODE=ALGORITHM)
REASON: <one sentence>
SOURCE: classifier | fail-safe
```

The executor reads this directly. **No regex fallback. No model judgment.** If `MODE` is MINIMAL or NATIVE, the executor uses the corresponding format from CLAUDE.md and stops. If `MODE` is ALGORITHM, the executor enters the Algorithm at the named `TIER`.

**Classifier rules (encoded in the hook's system prompt):**

- **MINIMAL** — greetings, ratings, single-token acknowledgments.
- **NATIVE** — single fact lookup OR single-line edit on a named file OR one command run, AND no new artifact created, AND no multi-step plan.
- **ALGORITHM** — everything else. Includes any build/create/make/implement/design/refactor/migrate/integrate request, anything touching multiple files, anything ambiguous, anything affecting doctrine/system-prompt/hooks/CLAUDE.md/Algorithm/ISA, anything spanning multiple projects, any meta-question about the system itself.
- **Tier (ALGORITHM only)** — E1 trivial (~<90s), E2 single-domain (~3min), E3 multi-file substantial (~10min), E4 cross-cutting/doctrine/architecture (~30min), E5 comprehensive (>2h). Bias higher when in doubt.

**Override hierarchy (executor side):**

1. Explicit `/e1`–`/e5` in the prompt forces tier (and forces ALGORITHM mode if MINIMAL/NATIVE was returned).
2. Otherwise honor classifier output verbatim.
3. **Conversation-context override:** if the classifier returns MINIMAL/NATIVE on a prompt that the conversation context makes clearly ALGORITHM-shaped (e.g., "yes" answering a multi-step proposal, "do it" approving an architecture change), the executor escalates to the appropriate tier and notes the mismatch in `## Decisions`. The classifier sees the prompt in isolation; the executor sees the thread.

**Fail-safe.** Any classifier error path — timeout (25s), non-zero exit, unparseable JSON — defaults to ALGORITHM E3 with `SOURCE: fail-safe` in REASON. Conservative-by-default: under-escalation is the failure mode this system was built to prevent.

**Telemetry.** Every classification is logged to `MEMORY/OBSERVABILITY/mode-classifier.jsonl` with prompt excerpt, mode, tier, reason, source, and latency. Audit weekly: classifier-vs-fail-safe ratio, average latency, downstream override rate.

**Coverage.** The classifier fires on `UserPromptSubmit` — top-level prompts only. Subagent prompts inherit whatever the primary picked. Sonnet latency adds ~3-8s per prompt; this is the deliberate cost of better judgment than regex could provide.

### ISC Quality System

**Every criterion describes one verifiable end-state.** The operational test is granularity:

> **Split until each criterion is one binary tool probe.** A criterion is granular enough when a single tool call (`Read`, `Grep`, `Bash`, `curl`, screenshot, `SELECT`, `bun test`, etc.) returns yes/no on whether it's met. If you cannot name the probe, the criterion is not yet atomic — split it. If the criterion needs human judgment, name the tool-verifiable proxy that stands in for the judgment.

**Tier floor:** the granularity rule produces a natural N. At E2+, that N must meet the tier ISC floor (E2 ≥16, E3 ≥32, E4 ≥128, E5 ≥256). For complex-app project ISAs, the ISC count naturally runs much higher. E1 has no floor — fast-path stays fast.

**Splitting Test** — apply to every criterion as you write it:

| Test | Split when... |
|------|--------------|
| "And"/"With" | Joins two verifiable things |
| Independent failure | Part A can pass while B fails |
| Scope words | "all", "every", "complete" → enumerate |
| Domain boundary | Crosses UI/API/data/logic → one per boundary |
| **No nameable probe** | You can't say which tool would verify it |

**Format:** `- [ ] ISC-N: criterion text` — the criterion phrasing reveals its category. **All ISCs number sequentially as `ISC-N`** — anti-criteria included. ID-stability rule applies: never re-number on edit; splits become `ISC-N.M`.

**Two doctrinal ISC kinds preserved as prose prefix conventions:**

| Kind | Surface form | Rule |
|------|--------------|------|
| **Anti-criterion** — must NOT happen | `- [ ] ISC-N: Anti: <what must NOT happen>` | **≥1 required** |
| **Antecedent** — precondition for target experience | `- [ ] ISC-N: Antecedent: <precondition>` | **≥1 required when goal is experiential** |

**For complex-app projects: the ISA test surface includes (non-exhaustive):**
- **Functional** — features work end-to-end
- **API** — endpoints exist, return expected shape, handle errors
- **Auth** — sign-in/out, token expiry, magic-link flow, session lifecycle
- **Authorization (RBAC/visibility)** — role X can/cannot reach endpoint Y
- **Performance** — latency budgets per route, bundle sizes, query times
- **Security model** — input validation, output encoding, CSRF, rate limits, secret handling
- **Data integrity** — schema invariants, foreign-key consistency, idempotency
- **Build & deploy** — `bun build` succeeds, typecheck clean, deploy version matches
- **Operational** — `/health` returns 200, error budget within SLO, synthetic monitor up

These aren't "in addition to" the ISA — they ARE the ISA. The ISA is the test harness because the ISCs are the tests.

**Allowed status markers:**
- `- [ ]` — pending, not yet verified
- `- [x]` — passed, verified with evidence
- `- [DEFERRED-VERIFY]` — passed in code/intent but live probe is impossible at execution time. **Requires a follow-up task ID in the verification notes.** Cannot be marked `[x]` until the deferred probe runs.

#### 🩻 Root-Cause-at-Ingestion Checkpoint

Before committing to ANY fix that modifies output-side behavior, answer in ISA `## Decisions` (use `Skill("ISA", "append decision ...")` for canonical entry):

1. **Where does this bad state enter the system?** Name the ingestion point.
2. **If I fix it at the ingestion point instead of here, do 3 similar bugs disappear?** If yes → move the fix upstream.
3. **Am I tracing database-up or display-down?** For UI bugs, the Reproduce-First rule forces display-down.

### 🧪 INLINE VERIFICATION MANDATE

**No ISC criterion may transition `[ ]` → `[x]` without verification evidence captured in the same tool call block that claims it, or the immediately-following block.**

| ISC type | Minimum verification tool call |
|----------|-------------------------------|
| File write | `Read` the file and confirm expected content |
| Code edit | `Grep` for the new symbol/line, or `Read` the specific range |
| Command execution | `Bash` with the actual command and checked output |
| HTTP/API change | `curl -i` with status + body shape check |
| Deploy | Live URL `curl` or `Interceptor` screenshot showing deployed version |
| UI change | `Skill("Interceptor")` screenshot at the target route |
| Schema/DB change | `SELECT` confirming the migration landed |
| Config/env change | Read-back of the file confirming the new value is on disk |

Evidence in ISA `## Verification`:

```

Use `Skill("ISA", "append verification to <isa-path>: ISC-N <probe-type> <evidence>")` to ensure canonical format.

**Forbidden language**: "should work", "should be", "expected to", "the change is in place" (without Read/Grep), "done" (without tool evidence), "no errors" (without the actual log).

Every `[ ]`→`[x]` ISC transition fires `CheckpointPerISC.hook.ts`. For each repo in `~/.claude/checkpoint-repos.txt` with uncommitted changes, the hook auto-commits. Idempotent via sidecar `MEMORY/WORK/{slug}/.checkpoint-state.json`. (v6.2.x: hook will also fire on `<project>/ISA.md` edits once isa-utils discovery lands.)

### 🛡️ VERIFICATION DOCTRINE

Four rules govern every VERIFY pass.

#### Rule 1 — Live-Probe for User-Facing Artifacts

**If the ISC criterion covers a user-facing artifact, mark it passed ONLY with tool-verified probe evidence.**

| Artifact type | Required probe |
|---------------|----------------|
| Web page / UI | Browser screenshot via `Skill("Interceptor")` |
| HTTP endpoint | `curl` response with expected status + body shape |
| CLI tool output | Actual stdout captured |
| Database write | Subsequent `SELECT` confirming the write |
| File write | `Read` confirming content matches intent |
| Hook / skill | Direct `bun run` invocation with synthetic input |
| Deploy | Verify deployed version string, not just successful push |

**"Should work," "looks fine," "tests pass" are NOT evidence for user-facing criteria.**

**Probe-impossible escape clause:** If a live probe is genuinely impossible at execution time, mark the criterion `[DEFERRED-VERIFY]` with a **required follow-up task ID**.

#### Rule 2 — Commitment-Boundary Advisor Calls

On **multi-step ISAs** (Extended+ effort, multi-file edits, architecture changes), call the advisor at:
1. **Before committing to an approach** — after PLAN, before BUILD begins on the main work
2. **When stuck or diverging** — if the same problem resists two distinct attempts
3. **Once after producing a durable deliverable** — before setting `phase: complete` in LEARN

```bash

69	## Problem
70	
71	The current incident categorisation model uses a category and type structure that has grown to a point where it creates ambiguity rather than clarity\. A single incident can reasonably be classified under multiple types\. Operators make different choices in the same situation, which degrades data consistency and makes it harder to report on, learn from, or compare incidents\. The distinction between what constitutes a type and what is really an attribute of the incident is unclear, leading to types that exist to capture information rather than to classify, and unclear practice across different operators\.
72	
73	## Proposed change
74	
75	Replace the current flat category and type model with an inheritance\-based approach\. A type can be a parent of another type, creating a clear decision tree that guides the operator to a single correct classification\.
76	
77	As part of this, separate what is genuinely an incident type from what is an attribute \(called a Tag in the model design\)\. Attributes describe characteristics of the incident, for example a SUP was involved or envenomation occurred\. Types classify the nature of the incident itself\.
78	
79	The outcome is fewer types overall, a clear path from general to specific, a clear process for how an incident record should evolve, and no scenario where an operator is choosing between two equally valid options\. This should result in consistent categorisation regardless of operator or surrounding circumstances\.
80	
81	## Impact
82	
83	- Consistent classification across operators, shifts, and states
84	- Cleaner data for reporting, trend analysis, and benchmarking
85	- Faster incident creation, as operators follow a decision tree rather than a long list
86	- A foundation of both capability and process for future initiatives and features that rely on structured, predictable data
87

90	Simplification and Cohesion\.

94	- This brief is project 1\.1 specifically, but is closely linked to Simplified Incident Creation \(prerequisite\) and Incident Tags \(extension\)\.

96	
97	## Design questions and where they landed
98	
99	The questions this brief opened with, and their current state\. The Model Design in this pack carries the detail\.
100	
101	1. __Where is the line between a type and an attribute?__ Proposed in full\. A value is a Type only if it changes what the incident fundamentally is\. Otherwise it is a Tag, a Status, an Outcome, or clinical detail\. See Model Design, Separation of concerns\.
102	2. __What does the type hierarchy look like?__ Proposed in full\. See Model Design, Top\-level Type tree and Medical branch\.
103	3. __How does an incident record evolve as more is learned?__ Proposed in full\. The Type is only updated to correct miscategorisation, never because the incident evolved\. Evolution is carried by Agency Status, Incident Outcome, Tags, and the Incident Log\. See Model Design, Definitions\.
104	4. __How do we migrate without losing historical comparability?__ Drafted\. Every one of the 72 current types is mapped in the Migration Map\. Flagged rows remain open\.
105	5. __How does this interact with incident labels?__ Proposed in full\. Tags and the Incident Labels project \(priority 1\.8\) are one effort\. The full tag taxonomy is still to be drafted\.
106	6. __What is the minimum set of types, and how do we resist adding more?__ Proposed in full\. The governing rule plus the Abstract / Not Final / Final states keep the tree small\. Open to SME pressure\-testing\.

111	- Stand up the Incident Categorisation and Flow SME group and circulate this pack for input\.

114	# Model Design
115	
116	## Definitions
117	
118	__Incident\.__ A response by Life Saving Victoria members that either:
119	
120	- Requires a response from multiple lifesaving services, or
121	- Requires assistance from other emergency services, including all situations where there is a danger to human life, or
122	- Is otherwise serious or complex such that members would like support, assistance, and visibility from LSV Command\.
123	
124	__Event\.__ A major occurrence that results in, or has the potential to result in, multiple Incidents\. An Event is the vehicle for associating multiple different Incidents that share a common cause or context\. Not all incidents will require an event association\. Example: Wye River Floods\.
125	
126	__Incident Type\.__ The nature of the situation assets are responding to\. The Incident Type reflects the __primary driver__ of the situation, not everything that happens during it\. A rescue followed by first aid is still a Rescue\. A member presenting on the beach with a major first aid is a Medical incident\.
127	
128	__When to update an Incident Type\.__
129	
130	- Updated only when new information clarifies that the initial classification was incorrect\.
131	- The Type is not updated because the incident evolves over time\.
132	- The Type captures what we responded to, not what unfolded\. Evolution is captured in the Agency Status, Incident Outcome, Tags, and Incident Log\. This aligns with Ambulance Victoria practice, which does not recategorise unless the incident was misreported\.
133	
134	## Key Assumptions
135	
136	1. __Human first, vessel second\.__ Where a situation involves both people and a vessel, the Type follows the people\. A capsize with two people retrieved is a Rescue\. The vessel dimension be captured as tags and the log, not as the Type\.
137	2. __No priority codes\.__ MPDS surfaces ProQA determinant codes \(Delta, Charlie, Bravo, Alpha, Omega\)\. We do not adopt them\. For lifesaving, we are either responding or it is advisory\. That distinction is already carried primarily by the Agency Status \(advisory by Information Only, response covered by all other statuses\)\. A priority field would duplicate information the model already holds\.
138	3. __The Type is what we responded to\.__ Not what unfolded afterwards\. Updates only correct miscategorisation \(see Definitions\)\.
139	4. __Specificity comes from the tree walk, not the type count\.__ Guided questions drill to a child or set a Tag\.
140	
141	## Design goals
142	
143	- Simplification and clarity above all\.
144	- One incident, one type\. No situation should fit two types where it can be avoided\.
145	- Fewer types overall\. Specificity comes from a guided question flow, not a long list\.
146	- Full backwards compatibility\. Every current category and type maps cleanly to a new home, so historical data stays comparable\. National is likely to follow LSV's lead\.

__LIMSOC Incident Categorisation__

Operational Change Proposal, 9 July 2026

*LIMSOC\-BRIEF\-LSV\-2026\-XXX | Season 2026\-27 | Focus Area 1: Enhance Our Incident Management | Working draft, not yet SME\-circulated*

# About This Pack

This pack proposes a new incident categorisation model for LIMSOC, Life Saving Victoria's operational incident\-management system, and maps every current incident type to the new model\. 

__Status\.__ Working draft\. Nothing in this pack is endorsed yet\.

## How to read this pack

1. __Project Brief\.__ Why the current model needs to change, and what the change is\.
2. __Model Design\.__ The proposed model\. Definitions, the type tree, and the rules that govern classification\. This is the core of the pack\.
3. __Migration Map\.__ Every one of the 72 current LIMSOC incident types mapped to its new home\. Most rows follow mechanically from the model's rules\. Rows marked __FLAG__ need a decision\.
4. __Decision Log\.__ What has already been proposed as decision, and why, so settled points are not relitigated\.
5. __SME Feedback\.__ Where group input is logged as it arrives\.

## Next Steps

- Feedback and consultation\.

Feedback to Nicholas Wood, State Lifesaving Communications Officer\.

# Project Brief

__Field__

__Value__

brief\_id

LIMSOC\-BRIEF\-LSV\-2026\-001

project\_ref

1\.1 New Incident Categorisation

focus\_area

1\. Enhance Our Incident Management

season

2026\-27

status

draft

owner

Nicholas Wood

sme\_group

Incident Categorisation and Flow

themes

\[Simplification, Cohesion\]

last\_updated

2026\-07\-08

## Problem

The current incident categorisation model uses a category and type structure that has grown to a point where it creates ambiguity rather than clarity\. A single incident can reasonably be classified under multiple types\. Operators make different choices in the same situation, which degrades data consistency and makes it harder to report on, learn from, or compare incidents\. The distinction between what constitutes a type and what is really an attribute of the incident is unclear, leading to types that exist to capture information rather than to classify, and unclear practice across different operators\.

## Proposed change

Replace the current flat category and type model with an inheritance\-based approach\. A type can be a parent of another type, creating a clear decision tree that guides the operator to a single correct classification\.

As part of this, separate what is genuinely an incident type from what is an attribute \(called a Tag in the model design\)\. Attributes describe characteristics of the incident, for example a SUP was involved or envenomation occurred\. Types classify the nature of the incident itself\.

The outcome is fewer types overall, a clear path from general to specific, a clear process for how an incident record should evolve, and no scenario where an operator is choosing between two equally valid options\. This should result in consistent categorisation regardless of operator or surrounding circumstances\.

## Impact

- Consistent classification across operators, shifts, and states
- Cleaner data for reporting, trend analysis, and benchmarking
- Faster incident creation, as operators follow a decision tree rather than a long list
- A foundation of both capability and process for future initiatives and features that rely on structured, predictable data

## Themes

Simplification and Cohesion\.

## Scope notes

- This brief is project 1\.1 specifically, but is closely linked to Simplified Incident Creation \(prerequisite\) and Incident Tags \(extension\)\.
- The incident labels work \(1\.8\) is closely coupled, as moving descriptive metadata into labels is what keeps the type hierarchy clean\. Worth deciding upfront whether categorisation and labels are designed together\.

## Design questions and where they landed

The questions this brief opened with, and their current state\. The Model Design in this pack carries the detail\.

1. __Where is the line between a type and an attribute?__ Proposed in full\. A value is a Type only if it changes what the incident fundamentally is\. Otherwise it is a Tag, a Status, an Outcome, or clinical detail\. See Model Design, Separation of concerns\.
2. __What does the type hierarchy look like?__ Proposed in full\. See Model Design, Top\-level Type tree and Medical branch\.
3. __How does an incident record evolve as more is learned?__ Proposed in full\. The Type is only updated to correct miscategorisation, never because the incident evolved\. Evolution is carried by Agency Status, Incident Outcome, Tags, and the Incident Log\. See Model Design, Definitions\.
4. __How do we migrate without losing historical comparability?__ Drafted\. Every one of the 72 current types is mapped in the Migration Map\. Flagged rows remain open\.
5. __How does this interact with incident labels?__ Proposed in full\. Tags and the Incident Labels project \(priority 1\.8\) are one effort\. The full tag taxonomy is still to be drafted\.
6. __What is the minimum set of types, and how do we resist adding more?__ Proposed in full\. The governing rule plus the Abstract / Not Final / Final states keep the tree small\. Open to SME pressure\-testing\.

## Next steps

- Circulate for feedback with LIMSOC and EMCaR team\.
- Stand up the Incident Categorisation and Flow SME group and circulate this pack for input\.
- Capture decisions in the Decision Log as they are made\.

# Model Design

## Definitions

__Incident\.__ A response by Life Saving Victoria members that either:

- Requires a response from multiple lifesaving services, or
- Requires assistance from other emergency services, including all situations where there is a danger to human life, or
- Is otherwise serious or complex such that members would like support, assistance, and visibility from LSV Command\.

__Event\.__ A major occurrence that results in, or has the potential to result in, multiple Incidents\. An Event is the vehicle for associating multiple different Incidents that share a common cause or context\. Not all incidents will require an event association\. Example: Wye River Floods\.

__Incident Type\.__ The nature of the situation assets are responding to\. The Incident Type reflects the __primary driver__ of the situation, not everything that happens during it\. A rescue followed by first aid is still a Rescue\. A member presenting on the beach with a major first aid is a Medical incident\.

__When to update an Incident Type\.__

- Updated only when new information clarifies that the initial classification was incorrect\.
- The Type is not updated because the incident evolves over time\.
- The Type captures what we responded to, not what unfolded\. Evolution is captured in the Agency Status, Incident Outcome, Tags, and Incident Log\. This aligns with Ambulance Victoria practice, which does not recategorise unless the incident was misreported\.

## Key Assumptions

1. __Human first, vessel second\.__ Where a situation involves both people and a vessel, the Type follows the people\. A capsize with two people retrieved is a Rescue\. The vessel dimension be captured as tags and the log, not as the Type\.
2. __No priority codes\.__ MPDS surfaces ProQA determinant codes \(Delta, Charlie, Bravo, Alpha, Omega\)\. We do not adopt them\. For lifesaving, we are either responding or it is advisory\. That distinction is already carried primarily by the Agency Status \(advisory by Information Only, response covered by all other statuses\)\. A priority field would duplicate information the model already holds\.
3. __The Type is what we responded to\.__ Not what unfolded afterwards\. Updates only correct miscategorisation \(see Definitions\)\.
4. __Specificity comes from the tree walk, not the type count\.__ Guided questions drill to a child or set a Tag\.

## Design goals

- Simplification and clarity above all\.
- One incident, one type\. No situation should fit two types where it can be avoided\.
- Fewer types overall\. Specificity comes from a guided question flow, not a long list\.
- Full backwards compatibility\. Every current category and type maps cleanly to a new home, so historical data stays comparable\. National is likely to follow LSV's lead\.

## Separation of concerns

Every value attached to an incident answers exactly one of these questions\. The current approach covers all concerns with different types\.

__Question__

__Mechanism__

__Cardinality__

__Example__

What is it, fundamentally

Type \(inheritance tree\)

one

SAR, Rescue, Person

What qualifies or characterises it

Tags \(the Incident Labels work, priority 1\.8\)

many

Resuscitation, Rescue Completed, External Request

Where is it in the lifecycle

Agency Status

one at a time

Responding, On Scene, Under Control

How did it end

Incident Outcome

one, gated by Type

Resolved, False Alarm, Fatality, Located

Clinical detail

Linked First Aid record

as needed

resus, fracture, marine sting

Part of a bigger event

Event

one

Wye River Floods

Free\-form situational context

Incident Log

append\-only

narrative entries with author and time

Free\-form summary

Incident Name and Incident Brief

one each

short human\-readable identifiers

__Governing rule\.__ A value only earns its place as a Type if it changes what the incident fundamentally is\. Otherwise it is a Tag, a Status, an Outcome, or clinical detail\.

## Type states

A Type in the tree carries a state that governs when it can be used\.

__State__

__Can open as this?__

__Can close as this?__

__Purpose__

__Abstract__

No

No

Grouping node in the tree only\. Structure, not selection\. Used for reporting\.

__Not Final__

Yes

No

Can be opened when the specific nature is not yet known\. Must be refined to a Final child before closure\.

__Final__

Yes

Yes

Fully specific\. Terminal in the tree\.

For example:

- __Medical__ is Not Final\. An incident can be opened as Medical while the primary presenting problem is still being assessed\. Before closure it must be refined to Chest Pain, Drowning, Breathing Problems, and so on\.
- __Search and Rescue__ is Abstract\. A bare SAR cannot be opened\. One of its children must be selected\.
- __Chest Pain__ is Final\.

## Top\-level Type tree

- __Search And Rescue__ \[Abstract\]
- __Search__ \[Abstract\]
- Person \[Non\-Final\]
- Land \[Final\]
- Water \[Final\]
- Vessel \[Final\]
- __Rescue__ \[Abstract\]
- Person \[Non\-Final\]
- Land \[Final\]
- Water \[Final\]
- Vessel \[Final\]
- __Emergency__ \[Abstract\]
- Rescue Equipment Activation \[Final\]
- Duress Activation \[Final\]
- Flare Sighting \[Final\]
- __Welfare Check__
- __Medical__ \[Not Final\]
- MPDS\-aligned children\. See Medical branch below\.
- __External Agency__ \[Abstract\]
- Tasking \[Final\]
- Request for Assistance \[Final\]
- __Marine Incident__ \[Abstract\]
- __Vessel Incident__ \[Abstract\]
- Assist \[Final\]
- Report \[Final\]
- __Dangerous Animal__ \[Abstract\]
- Shark \[Final\]
- Other \[Final\]
- __Advisory Information__ \[Abstract\]
- Dangerous Conditions \[Final\]
- Equipment Fault \[Final\]
- Medication Discrepancy \[Final\]
- Operational Change \[Final\]

__Out of scope for the incident taxonomy\.__ Administrative items \(system status advisories, COVID\-era system messaging\) do not belong here\. They move out of the incident taxonomy entirely\.

__Activation handling\.__ When a Rescue Equipment Activation or Duress Activation leads to a real rescue, the incident stays as the activation Type it was opened as\. One incident, no reclassification, no second incident\. The rescue that follows is carried in Agency Status, Tags, Incident Outcome, and the log\.

## Guided questions

A Type may carry key questions, in the style of ProQA \(the scripted question flow used by MPDS dispatch systems\)\. Each answer does one of two things:

1. Drills to a child Type\.
2. Sets a controlled Tag\.

No per\-incident custom fields are created\. The questions populate the existing primitives \(Type and Tags\)\.

__Governance\.__ Questions are centrally defined per Type\. An answer maps to a child Type or a controlled Tag, never to free text that fragments data\. Keep a deliberately small set of true structured fields only where the value is quantitative and reporting critical \(for example, number of people involved\)\. Default everything else to Tags\.

## Agency Status \- Incident lifecycle

Captures our overall status as an agency\. These will include:

1. Collecting Information
2. Responding
3. On Scene
4. Under Control
5. Returning
6. Finalising
7. Information Only \- Monitoring, aware but no active response

## Incident Outcome

Captured as a required selection when closing an incident\. Controlled and mutually exclusive per Type\.

For example, a Search Type surfaces:

- Located
- Fatality
- Stood Down

A Medical Type surfaces:

- Resolved
- Referred to Agency
- Fatality

A Rescue Equipment Activation surfaces the same outcomes as a Rescue, with the additional outcome of False Alarm\.

## One Type per incident

- Type captures the primary operational driver\.
- Clinical detail always rides in the linked First Aid Log, never as a competing Type\. A rescue that becomes a resuscitation is one Rescue incident with a resus FAL\.
- Multiple separate responses to one situation group under an Event\. They are not merged into one incident\.

Where two operational drivers genuinely co\-occur, precedence selects the Type:

1. Search and Rescue or Rescue \(a save wins\)
2. Marine Incident
3. Medical
4. Advisory Information

__Worked scenarios\.__

1. __Rescue then major medical\.__ Swimmer pulled from a rip, arrests on the beach\. Type is Rescue\. Resuscitation rides as a Tag \(FA form required\) and in the FAL\.
2. __Vessel incident producing a rescue\.__ Capsized vessel, people retrieved\. Type is Rescue\. Human first, vessel second\. The vessel dimension is Tags and log\.
3. __Medical during an External Agency Tasking\.__ Severity decides\. A severe injury becomes its own linked incident\. A minor one stays on the Tasking incident with a Member Injury Tag\.
4. __Activation that becomes a rescue\.__ Stays one incident, typed as the activation \(for example Duress Activation\)\. See Activation handling above\.

## Tasking versus Incident

This is determined by our response\. Are we responding to provide our services independently? This may include as part of an interagency response\. Or are we responding to support the services of another agency\.

- We are delivering services, we open an incident of the appropriate type\.
- If we are assisting other agencies to perform their duties, this is an external agency \- tasking incident\.

Worked example\. AV asks us to help carry their patient off the beach\. We are a resource on AV's job, so __External Agency > Tasking__, with tags and log notes to capture details as required\. If instead we are managing the patient and called AV, it is __Medical__, and AV listed in responding services\.

Extrication is an action, so it is a Tag, never a Type\. This retires Assist Extrication as a Type\.

## Medical branch \(MPDS\-aligned\)

Medical children align to the Medical Priority Dispatch System \(MPDS\) chief complaints, as used by Ambulance Victoria\. MPDS is maintained by the International Academies of Emergency Dispatch \(IAED\)\. It is used here as a naming taxonomy for interagency alignment, not as a dispatch triage tool\.

__State\.__ Medical is __Not Final__\. Every closed Medical incident must be refined to a Final child\.

__Medical children \(all Final\)\.__

- Abdominal Pain / Problems
- Allergies \(Reactions\) / Envenomations \(Stings, Bites\)\. Marine envenomation rides here, animal identity as a Tag

## Tags

Tags characterise\. They never classify\. Draft groups:

__Care and clinical, first\-aid\-form triggers\.__

- Resuscitation → FA form required
- Member Injury → FA form required
- Penthrane Administered → FA form required
- Major First Aid → FA form required
- Oxygen Administered → FA form required
- Rescue Completed → Rescue form required\. The Rescue form must capture method \(including Heli rescue technique\) and that data must flow back to the incident record\. Requirement on the platform\.

__Operational context\.__

- External Request \(a request originating outside LSV, distinct from the External Agency > Request for Assistance Type\)
- Off\-duty response
- Multi\-agency
- Extrication
- Mass Rescue \(scale tag on a Rescue or SAR\)

__Vessel Incident modifiers\.__

- Injury / No Injury

__Dangerous Animal modifiers\.__

- Confirmed / Reported
- Confirmation source \(Lifeguard, Aerial, Member of public, External agency\)

## Platform dev notes

Design constraints the platform must support\.

__Required documentation rules\.__

- Set required documents against an Incident Type\. Inputs can include People \(for example, patient count\)\.
- Set required documents against Incident Tags\.
- Distinguish between "form submission required" and "specific section within a form required"\.

__Tag scoping\.__

- Constrain Tags to specific Incident Types by inclusion or exclusion\. A Tag that only makes sense for Medical should not appear on a Marine Incident\.

__Type states, platform behaviour\.__

- Types are Abstract, Not Final, or Final\. See Type states above\.
- Abstract Types cannot be selected on open or close\.
- Not Final Types can be opened but not closed\. The user is prompted to refine before Finalising\.
- Final Types can be opened and closed\.

## Backwards compatibility

Every current category and type maps to exactly one new home: a Type, a Tag, an Agency Status, an Incident Outcome, or a linked\-record concept\. Nothing is lost\.

Category\-level map:

- SAR → Search And Rescue > Search or Rescue, refined to Final child\.
- MED → Medical \(Not Final\), refined to an MPDS\-aligned Final child before closure\.
- VINC → Marine Incident > Vessel Incident > Assist or Report\. Injury moves to Outcome and Tag\.
- RESC → Search And Rescue > Rescue\. Injury or no injury moves out of the Type onto the linked FAL\.
- SHARK → Marine Incident > Dangerous Animal > Shark\. Confirmation and source as Tags\.
- DUR → Search And Rescue > Emergency > Duress Activation\. Accidental as a Tag\.
- Rescue Equipment Activation → Search And Rescue > Emergency > Rescue Equipment Activation\.
- TASK → External Agency > Tasking\.
- BAU → splits across Advisory Information, External Agency, and out\-of\-scope admin\.
- FA → Incident Outcome False Alarm, not a Type\.
- INC → decomposes into the proper branches above\.
- MR \(Mass Rescue\) → scale Tag on a Rescue or SAR\.

The full per\-type map, covering all 72 current types, is in the Migration Map\.

Base directory for this skill: /home/nicholas-wood/.claude/skills/IterativeDepth

## Customization

**Before executing, check for user customizations at:**
`~/.claude/PAI/USER/SKILLCUSTOMIZATIONS/IterativeDepth/`

If this directory exists, load and apply any PREFERENCES.md, configurations, or resources found there. These override default behavior. If the directory does not exist, proceed with skill defaults.


# IterativeDepth

**Structured multi-angle exploration of the same problem to extract deeper understanding and richer ISC criteria.**

Grounded in 20 established scientific techniques across cognitive science (Hermeneutic Circle, Triangulation), AI/ML (Self-Consistency, Ensemble Methods), requirements engineering (Viewpoint-Oriented RE), and design thinking (Six Thinking Hats, Causal Layered Analysis).

## Core Concept

Instead of analyzing a problem once, run 2-8 structured passes through the same problem, each from a systematically different **lens**. Each pass surfaces requirements, edge cases, and criteria invisible from other angles. The combination yields ISC criteria that no single-pass analysis could produce.

## Use / Win

**When to use:** Any time you have time budget beyond Standard tier and the task is important enough that getting the ISC right matters more than speed. This is the single most valuable thinking capability for the OBSERVE phase. If you're at Extended effort or above, you should be asking "why NOT use IterativeDepth?" rather than "why use it?"

Concrete triggers:
- **Extra time available** — Extended+ effort means you have the budget. Spend it on understanding the problem deeply before writing ISC, not on writing more code faster.
- **Deep analysis of what's actually being asked** — The user said X. But what do they actually need? What are they trying to accomplish? What would make them rate this 9-10? Single-pass reverse engineering catches the obvious. IterativeDepth catches the rest.
- **Different angles of approach** — Before committing to an approach, explore the problem from stakeholder, failure, temporal, experiential, and constraint-inversion angles. The right approach often only becomes obvious after seeing the problem from 3-4 directions.
- **Important or critical tasks** — When the user says "this is critical" or the task has high blast radius, the cost of missing a dimension is much higher than the cost of 2-5 extra minutes of analysis.
- **Tasks you've never done before** — Novel work has the highest density of hidden requirements. IterativeDepth is insurance against the things you don't know you don't know.

**What you win:**
- **ISC criteria that single-pass analysis cannot produce.** Each lens surfaces requirements invisible from other angles. A 4-lens pass routinely discovers 30-50% more criteria than direct analysis.
- **Blind spot elimination before they become mid-EXECUTE surprises.** Rework from missed requirements is 5-10x more expensive than the upfront analysis. IterativeDepth pays for itself by preventing restarts.
- **Approach clarity.** Seeing the problem from failure, stakeholder, and constraint-inversion angles often reveals that the obvious approach is wrong and a better path exists.
- **Confidence.** When ISC criteria are built on multi-angle analysis, you can execute with conviction instead of discovering gaps halfway through.

**The default mental model should be:** At Extended+ effort, IterativeDepth is not optional enrichment — it's the standard way to understand what you're building before you build it.

## Workflow Routing

| Trigger | Workflow |
|---------|----------|
| "iterative depth", "explore deeper", "multi-angle" | `Workflows/Explore.md` |
| "quick depth", "fast angles" | `Workflows/Explore.md` (Fast mode: 2 lenses) |

## Quick Reference

- **8 Lenses** available, scaled by SLA (2-8)
- **Each lens** is a structurally different exploration angle
- **Output** is new/refined ISC criteria per pass
- **Integration** point: Deeper understanding through structured multi-angle analysis

**Full Documentation:**
- Scientific grounding: `ScientificFoundation.md`
- Lens definitions: `TheLenses.md`

## Gotchas

- **2-8 lens passes, not infinite.** Diminishing returns after ~5 passes for most topics.
- **Each pass should surface genuinely NEW requirements, not restate previous findings.** If passes start repeating, stop early.
- **This is a BPE-fragile skill.** Monitor whether smarter models make it unnecessary. Quarterly test recommended.

## Examples

**Example 1: Surface hidden requirements**
```
User: "use iterative depth on this API redesign"
→ Pass 1: Functional requirements
→ Pass 2: Security implications
→ Pass 3: Performance constraints
→ Pass 4: Backward compatibility
→ Each pass surfaces new requirements missed by previous
```

## Execution Log

After completing any workflow, append a single JSONL entry:

```bash
echo '{"ts":"'$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)'","skill":"IterativeDepth","workflow":"WORKFLOW_USED","input":"8_WORD_SUMMARY","status":"ok|error","duration_s":SECONDS}' >> ~/.claude/PAI/MEMORY/SKILLS/execution.jsonl
```

Replace `WORKFLOW_USED` with the workflow executed, `8_WORD_SUMMARY` with a brief input description, and `SECONDS` with approximate wall-clock time. Log `status: "error"` if the workflow failed.

# ISA — Incident Categorisation Pack Restructure

## Problem

The v0.7 pack (OneDrive 00_Inbox, 9 Jul 2026) cannot be read linearly — Nick jumps around when explaining it. Verified structural defects: "When to update an Incident Type" stated in Definitions then restated as Key Assumption 3; Type states explained before the tree they govern; Medical children referenced in the tree then listed in a separate branch section; Tasking-vs-Incident logic split between the tree (External Agency) and its own later section; guided-questions detail arrives before all fields are introduced; the why behind Outcome, Tags, and the type-freeze is asserted, not motivated. Principal feedback: too long and too technical for the senior manager of operations — "his eyes will glaze over." The document lacks the story Nick tells in person (first aid form precedent, comms-role evolution, rescue-becomes-drowning searchability failure, data-foundation benefits).

## Vision

A pack that reads start-to-finish following how an incident actually flows — challenge with the current structure, the proposed change, the impact, and what each audience will see — such that the senior manager of operations reads the front section cold and gets it, while the SME group still has every technical detail in annexes. Nick presents it without jumping around; the ~10 points he makes verbally are on the page.

## Out of Scope

- Changing the model design itself (tree, states, precedence, MPDS alignment) — this is a document restructure, not a model redesign.
- Resolving open model questions (D21 Welfare home, Not Final assignments) — they stay flagged.
- The full tag taxonomy (priority 1.8 work).
- Rollout/training collateral, unless Nick pulls change-management into scope (Q19).

## Constraints

- No content loss: all v0.7 technical material (migration map, decision log, platform dev notes, medical branch) survives somewhere.
- Discovery gate: no restructure outline or rewrite until Nick answers the discovery questions (this turn's deliverable).
- Outline approved by Nick before full rewrite.
- Markdown source in workspace; OneDrive receives exported .docx only, rendered programmatically, pushed via rclone copy.
- Australian English, no em dashes, executive-ready front narrative.

## Goal

Extract Nick's unstated points via targeted discovery questions, then restructure the pack into a flow-based narrative front (senior-manager-readable) with technical annexes (SME-grade), verified against every defect Nick named and every point extracted in discovery.

## Criteria

### Discovery (this turn)
- [ ] ISC-1: Question set delivered covering audience/artefact shape, incident-flow spine, in-person stories, quantified impact, content disposition, and scope
- [ ] ISC-2: Every question tied to a specific gap in v0.7 or a specific claim in Nick's word-dump
- [ ] ISC-3: Question set includes a mechanism to extract the "10 more points" (walk-through / voice-memo prompt)
- [ ] ISC-4: Highest-leverage questions flagged so Nick can answer partially and still unblock the outline
- [ ] ISC-5: No restructuring, rewriting, or file edits to the pack performed this turn

- [ ] ISC-7: Skeleton structured around the incident flow stages Nick confirms

━━━ 📃 SUMMARY ━━━ 7/7

🔄 ITERATION on: Round-1 answers absorbed; flow-spine dropped; second question set to close remaining gaps.

📃 CONTENT:

**A. React to a candidate shape (recommendation first — tear it apart)**
1. ★ Based on everything you've said, here's the arc I'd propose. React section by section — what's wrong, missing, or misordered?
   1. **The problem** — told through the stories: the same incident reasonably typed three different ways; operators diverging because no field is defined anywhere; a type changed mid-incident (rescue → drowning) making Major Rescues unsearchable; season data that takes days of manual interrogation to trust.
   2. **Why now, why us** — comms no longer signs on every unit; the job now is getting the data right. And we've done this before: the first aid form went from not-fit-for-purpose to giving us visibility we'd never had.
   3. **The fix in one idea** — every value on an incident answers exactly one question. Type = what we responded to. Status = where we are. Outcome = how it ended. Tags = what characterised it. FAL = clinical detail. The separation-of-concerns table becomes the centrepiece, with a written definition for every field for the first time.
   4. **The model, sold contextually** — the tree (with medical children in place and the removal justifications), type states, the type-freeze rule, precedence — each introduced by the problem it solves and anchored with a worked scenario, not stated spec-style.
   5. **What changes for you** — operators get a guided path instead of a 72-item list; duty officers get a cleaner common operating picture; leadership gets reporting they can finally rely on.
   6. **The bigger picture** — the foundation this lays (guided questions, AI-enabled features), and with the first aid form work, a cohesive, industry-leading package LSV can proudly share with the other states.
   7. **Annexes** — Migration Map, Decision Log, Platform dev notes, SME feedback.
2. "Sell the detail contextually" — is the mechanism per-concept worked scenarios (a real incident anchoring each rule)? v0.7 already has four good ones. Should every non-obvious rule get one?

**B. The stories still missing (carried forward, sharpened)**
3. ★ First aid form specifics: what did the old form fail to ask, what does the new one capture, and what's one concrete "we now know X, we could never see that before"? That single sentence is what makes the precedent land.
4. ★ Recurring objections: what pushback comes up every time you explain this? ("Fewer types loses detail", "more work at closure", "why AV's medical names", anything else.) Each one earns a pre-emptive answer in the doc.
5. Same-incident-different-types: which collisions actually bite today? From the migration map I'd guess Recovered from Water vs Rescue vs Drowning Death, and Marine Incident (Injury) vs Rescue. Which ones do you actually see operators split on?
6. The season data pull: who does it, for which report and audience (board, LSV exec, SLSA national?), and roughly how much manual effort? Even a ballpark ("a week of evenings each season") makes the impact real.

**C. Placement calls**
7. The comms-role evolution — does it open the document (the frame for why this matters), or sit inside "why now"?
8. On top of per-concept scenarios, is a single running incident woven start to finish (rip rescue → arrest → fatality, exercising type-freeze, tags, FAL, outcome, reporting) worth it, or is that one device too many?
9. Incident vs rescue log: v0.7 never defines the rescue log boundary. Does this pack define it (it's one of your core inconsistency stories), or do we name the problem and point to it as follow-on work?
10. "Design questions and where they landed" and "Still open" — fold into the Decision Log annex, or keep visible in the body as an honesty signal that this is a draft inviting SME input?

**D. Practicalities**
11. Volunteer leadership — who specifically (LSOCE, duty officers, club leadership?), and is there a forum or date this needs to hit for endorsement?
12. Source of truth: I only have the .docx. Is there a markdown source somewhere in the workspace, or do I create the markdown as the canonical source and export the .docx to OneDrive from it?

🖊️ STORY: Round one reshaped the brief substantially. Flow-spine dropped, contextual selling is the game. Candidate arc proposed plus eleven sharpened gap questions. Answers unlock the restructure outline next.

message.content: I like the drafted flow. Think a guiding principle behind the new document is that nothing gets repeated. And related concepts are together. For the second point the new arc will go a long way to capturing it, but using stories and examples where we can and reasons why, for example the structure. 4.3. We used to just ask a small set of basic questions. Quite often the questions didn't mention what didn't allow the operator the member to put in details relative to the incident. New form now presents questions depending on what happened. So if they tick that they use oxygen, then they get the oxygen questions. For the footpoint four, what's the recurring objection? Probably the biggest objection or the biggest thing I feel I need to sell is that there is a lot of detail here, but it is a complex problem. People have spoken for years that we need to redo it, but they haven't been able to do it. So there is a lot to it, but once you understand it, it's quite a simple solution. But say aside from that I get a lot of questions that the structural help answer better rather than objection. The key thing I need to sell here in terms of objections is that whilst this is a change, it's already broken and we can't get any worse than we currently are. Marine incident versus other vessel incident is a common one that we run into. Pretty much everything is generalized to a rescue in water condition unknown. There is no guidance on whether we make a rescue incident or a vessel incident. Recovered from water versus resuscitation is unclear. Currently we would have no idea if a resuscitation was something we came across on the beach or someone that we have pulled from the water. Also wouldn't know if we are assisting external and external agencies with our service or we are providing our assets. There is no consistent way to how an incident type should be updated or when it should be updated, so sometimes it's updated, sometimes it's not. Very much left to individuals' decisions, individuals experience and what it pe different people think should happen, which leads to inconsistency. Data that we now need to pull and manually do, it's currently done by the MCAR team and takes a lot of time to do everything from data for SLSA to data for councils to data for LSV and our clubs and services. Moving to point seven, the comms roll evolution, it doesn't open the document, it's just a why now, it's a supporting point, not a key point for number eight, that would be too much. Let's leave that out. Point nine, no we don't. This is a new thing that I need to include in the document. I want to merge the first aid form and the rescue log into one so that we have one action log and that is filled out no matter what. So in that table it'd be an action log which would be the assistance we provide to one individual. That may be a rescue, it may be a first aid, it may be both. By bringing these together we only have to put that person's details in once and it's really clear for our members that they need to do one action log for each person helped. If it is a major situation that meets the criteria for an incident, then all those action logs can be linked to an incident the way we do at the moment. So it's probably an expansion on the clinical notes thing in the separation of concerns table. Put the decisions into the annex. Volunteer leadership is our duty officer group, our LSV Comms Group and our Life-Saving Operations Council Council leadership team. The document should be taken as the source of truth at the moment. There may be a markdown that you can have a look for, but it's probably out of date. Terms of deadline, I want to get it in front of the senior manager operations this week, so hence why I would like to restructure the document
