content.text:
━━━ 📃 SUMMARY ━━━ 7/7

🔄 ITERATION on: Round-2 answers complete discovery; formulating the restructure plan you originally asked for.

📃 CONTENT:

**The restructure plan.** Discovery is done — this is the section-by-section skeleton, what moves where, and what gets written new. Per your original brief, I'm presenting it and stopping for approval before touching the document.

**New document skeleton**

**Part 1 — The case for change** *(new writing, built from your stories)*
- 1.1 *The problem.* No field has a written definition; the incident type is trying to be everything to everyone. Told through the real collisions: Marine Incident vs Vessel Incident with no guidance; everything defaulting to Rescue (In Water) Condition Unknown; Recovered from Water vs Resuscitation (we cannot tell a beach resus from a water retrieval); assisting an agency vs providing our service; type updates left to individual judgment (the rescue-that-becomes-a-drowning making Major Rescues unsearchable). The cost: EMCaR manually interrogating season data for SLSA, councils, LSV, clubs and services.
- 1.2 *Why now.* People have said for years this needs redoing; it has never been done because it is genuinely complex. The comms role has evolved (supporting point: sign-on is automated, the job now is getting the data right). And we have the precedent: the first aid form went from a small static question set that never matched what happened, to adaptive questions that follow the incident (tick oxygen, get the oxygen questions), and gave us visibility we had never had. The posture: this is a change, but the current state is already broken — we cannot get worse, only better.

**Part 2 — The proposal** *(existing material, restructured and sold contextually)*
- 2.1 *One idea.* Every value on an incident answers exactly one question — the separation-of-concerns table becomes the centrepiece, now with a written definition per field for the first time. The v0.7 Definitions section (Incident, Event) merges in here. The clinical-detail row becomes the **Action Log** (see 2.6). "Complex problem, simple solution once you understand it" is the framing sentence.
- 2.2 *The type tree.* Tree with type states explained inline where the tree first needs them (Abstract/Not Final/Final move here from their current position before the tree). Medical children in place in the tree section with the MPDS alignment rationale and the justification for each removal. Catch-all retirement (E99/D99/B99 → Not Final mechanism) told here as a story: the catch-alls existed because the old model gave no better home.
- 2.3 *The rules that make the data consistent.* All classification rules in one place, each as problem → rule → worked example: the type is what we responded to (freeze rule, stated here and only here, with the drowning example and the searchable-outcome payoff); one type per incident + precedence (human first, vessel second); tasking vs incident (resolves the assist-vs-provide ambiguity); activation handling. Key Assumptions dissolves — each assumption relocates into the rule it belongs to.
- 2.4 *Status, Outcome, Tags.* Each introduced by what it captures that the type no longer has to: lifecycle, how it ended (searchable at last), characteristics. Tag groups summarised; the full draft list can sit here or annex — I'll judge by weight during the rewrite.
- 2.5 *Guided questions.* Trimmed to the concept and the governance rule; positioned as the bridge to the future (2.7).
- 2.6 *The Action Log* **(new writing)**. First aid form and rescue log merge into one log: the assistance we provide to one individual — rescue, first aid, or both. Person's details entered once; one action log per person helped, every time; linked to an incident when the incident criteria are met. Resolves the incident-vs-rescue-log inconsistency named in Part 1.
- 2.7 *What this enables.* Foundation framing: guided questions, AI-enabled features, lifting expectations as the natural byproduct.

**Part 3 — What you will see** *(new writing)*
Operators: a guided path and clear definitions instead of a 72-item list. Duty officers: a consistent common operating picture. Leadership and reporting: data that can be relied on without manual interrogation — EMCaR's season pulls become queries, not projects. Closing frame: with the first aid form work, this presents a cohesive, industry-leading picture LSV can be proud to share with the other states.

**Part 4 — Next steps.** SME group, feedback process, decision capture. "Still open" items (tree confirmation, Not Final assignments, D21 Welfare) stay visible here as the honest invitation for input.

**Annexes.** A: Migration Map (all 72 rows, FLAG rows intact). B: Decision Log + "Design questions and where they landed" folded in; FAL-naming decision marked superseded by the Action Log. C: Platform dev notes (+ Action Log platform implications). D: SME feedback log.

**Duplication resolutions:** type-update rule stated once (2.3, removed from Definitions and Key Assumptions); type states once (2.2); medical children once (2.2); tasking-vs-incident once (2.3); Key Assumptions and Definitions dissolve into their homes. Verified by grep at the end — nothing repeated is ISC-38 in the working ISA.

**Three flags before I write:**
1. **Action Log depth** — full proposal treatment (problem, proposal, platform implications) or a deliberate one-page introduction flagged as "new in v0.8, detail to follow"? It's a second structural change with its own platform work; I'd recommend the one-page introduction so it doesn't unbalance the pack. Your call.
2. **Source reconciliation** — the workspace markdown (edited 14 Jul) looks current with the v0.7 docx; I'll diff to confirm and reconcile any docx-only edits before rewriting. If the docx has changes the markdown lacks, docx wins.
3. **Version and title** — I'd ship this as v0.8 under the same title. Confirm.

109

119	Captures our overall status as an agency. These will include:
120	
121	1. Collecting Information
122	2. Responding
123	3. On Scene
124	4. Under Control
125	5. Returning
126	6. Finalising

136	- Fatality

154	
155	1. Search and Rescue or Rescue (a save wins)
156	2. Marine Incident
157	3. Medical
158	4. Advisory Information

161	
162	1. **Rescue then major medical.** Swimmer pulled from a rip, arrests on the beach. Type is Rescue. Resuscitation rides as a Tag (FA form required) and in the FAL.
163	2. **Vessel incident producing a rescue.** Capsized vessel, people retrieved. Type is Rescue. Human first, vessel second. The vessel dimension is Tags and log.
164	3. **Shark sighting forcing water clearance.** Type stays Marine Incident > Dangerous Animal > Shark. The active response is carried by Agency Status, not a Type change.
165	4. **Medical during an External Agency Tasking.** Severity decides. A severe injury becomes its own linked incident. A minor one stays on the Tasking incident with a Member Injury Tag.
166	5. **Activation that becomes a rescue.** Stays one incident, typed as the activation (for example Duress Activation). See Activation handling above.
167

169	
170	This is determined by our response. Are we responding to provide our services independently? This may include as part of an interagency response. Or are we responding to support the services of another agency.
171	
172	- We are delivering services, we open an incident of the appropriate type.
173	- If we are assisting other agencies to perform their duties, this is an external agency incident.

190	- Assault / Sexual Assault
191	- Back Pain (Non-Traumatic / Non-Recent)
192	- Breathing Problems
193	- Burns (Scalds) / Explosions
194	- Carbon Monoxide / Inhalation / HAZMAT / CBRN
195	- Cardiac or Respiratory Arrest / Death
196	- Chest Pain
197	- Choking
198	- Convulsions / Seizures
199	- Diabetic Problems
200	- Drowning / Diving / SCUBA Accident
201	- Electrocution / Lightning
202	- Eye Problems / Injuries
203	- Falls
204	- Headache
205	- Heat / Cold Exposure
206	- Hemorrhage / Lacerations
207	- Overdose / Poisoning (Ingestion)
208	- Stab / Gunshot / Penetrating Trauma
209	- Stroke (CVA) / Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)
210	- Traumatic Injuries
211	- Unconscious / Fainting (Near)
212	- Unknown Problem (Collapse, 3rd Party)

215

226	
227	Tags characterise. They never classify. Draft groups:
228	
229	**Care and clinical, first-aid-form triggers.**
230	
231	- Resuscitation → FA form required
232	- Member Injury → FA form required
233	- Penthrane Administered → FA form required
234	- Major First Aid → FA form required
235	- Oxygen Administered → FA form required
236	- Rescue Completed → Rescue form required. The Rescue form must capture method (including Heli rescue technique) and that data must flow back to the incident record. Requirement on the platform.
237	
238	**Operational context.**
239	
240	- External Request (a request originating outside LSV, distinct from the External Agency > Request for Assistance Type)
241	- Off-duty response
242	- Multi-agency
243	- Extrication
244	- Mass Rescue (scale tag on a Rescue or SAR)
245	
246	**Vessel Incident modifiers.**
247	
248	- Injury / No Injury
249	
250	**Dangerous Animal modifiers.**
251	
252	- Confirmed / Reported
253	- Confirmation source (Lifeguard, Aerial, Member of public, External agency)

257	Design constraints the platform must support.
258	
259	**Required documentation rules.**
260	
261	- Set required documents against an Incident Type. Inputs can include People (for example, patient count).
262	- Set required documents against Incident Tags.
263	- Distinguish between "form submission required" and "specific section within a form required".
264	
265	**Tag scoping.**
266	
267	- Constrain Tags to specific Incident Types by inclusion or exclusion. A Tag that only makes sense for Medical should not appear on a Marine Incident.
268	
269	**Type states, platform behaviour.**
270	
271	- Types are Abstract, Not Final, or Final. See Type states above.
272	- Abstract Types cannot be selected on open or close.
273	- Not Final Types can be opened but not closed. The user is prompted to refine before Finalising.
274	- Final Types can be opened and closed.
275	
276	## Backwards compatibility
277	
278	Every current category and type maps to exactly one new home: a Type, a Tag, an Agency Status, an Incident Outcome, or a linked-record concept. Nothing is lost.
279	
280	Category-level map:
281	
282	- SAR → Search And Rescue > Search or Rescue, refined to Final child.
283	- MED → Medical (Not Final), refined to an MPDS-aligned Final child before closure.
284	- VINC → Marine Incident > Vessel Incident > Assist or Report. Injury moves to Outcome and Tag.
285	- RESC → Search And Rescue > Rescue. Injury or no injury moves out of the Type onto the linked FAL.
286	- SHARK → Marine Incident > Dangerous Animal > Shark. Confirmation and source as Tags.
287	- DUR → Search And Rescue > Emergency > Duress Activation. Accidental as a Tag.
288	- Rescue Equipment Activation → Search And Rescue > Emergency > Rescue Equipment Activation.
289	- TASK → External Agency > Tasking.
290	- BAU → splits across Advisory Information, External Agency, and out-of-scope admin.
291	- FA → Incident Outcome False Alarm, not a Type.
292	- INC → decomposes into the proper branches above.
293	- MR (Mass Rescue) → scale Tag on a Rescue or SAR.
294	
295	The full per-type map, covering all 72 current types, is in the Migration Map.
296	
297	## Still open
298	
299	1. Confirm the top-level tree structure (SAR / Medical / External Agency / Marine Incident / Advisory Information).
300	2. Confirm the Abstract / Not Final / Final assignment on each node. Medical as Not Final in particular, and whether SAR and Marine Incident should also be Not Final for the early window when the specific nature is unknown.

**Medical children (all Final).**

- Abdominal Pain / Problems
- Allergies (Reactions) / Envenomations (Stings, Bites). Marine envenomation rides here, animal identity as a Tag
- Animal Bites / Attacks
- Assault / Sexual Assault
- Back Pain (Non-Traumatic / Non-Recent)
- Breathing Problems
- Burns (Scalds) / Explosions
- Carbon Monoxide / Inhalation / HAZMAT / CBRN
- Cardiac or Respiratory Arrest / Death
- Chest Pain
- Choking
- Convulsions / Seizures
- Diabetic Problems
- Drowning / Diving / SCUBA Accident
- Electrocution / Lightning
- Eye Problems / Injuries
- Falls
- Headache
- Heat / Cold Exposure
- Hemorrhage / Lacerations
- Overdose / Poisoning (Ingestion)
- Stab / Gunshot / Penetrating Trauma
- Stroke (CVA) / Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)
- Traumatic Injuries
- Unconscious / Fainting (Near)
- Unknown Problem (Collapse, 3rd Party)

**Cut from the MPDS list, with reason.**

- Stun Gun component of the Assault compound. Not our operating context.
- Pandemic / Epidemic / Outbreak (Surveillance or Triage). Not the incident taxonomy. Sits in Advisory Information or system-level messaging if it ever needs a home.
- Inter-Facility Transfer / Palliative Care and Inter-Facility Transfer for medically trained callers. Patient transfer is not our operating context.
- Removed on review, 2026-07-09: Heart Problems / AICD, Inaccessible Incident / Entrapments, Pregnancy / Childbirth / Miscarriage, Psychiatric / Suicide Attempt, Sick Person, Traffic / Transportation Incidents, Automatic Crash Notification (ACN), HCP (Health-Care Practitioner) Referral.

**Priority codes.** Not adopted. See Design assumptions.

**Marine envenomation, worked.** A bluebottle sting is Type = Medical > Allergies (Reactions) / Envenomations (Stings, Bites), Tag = Marine Envenomation, Tag = Bluebottle.

## Tags

Tags characterise. They never classify. Draft groups:

**Care and clinical, first-aid-form triggers.**

- Resuscitation → FA form required
- Member Injury → FA form required
- Penthrane Administered → FA form required
- Major First Aid → FA form required
- Oxygen Administered → FA form required
- Rescue Completed → Rescue form required. The Rescue form must capture method (including Heli rescue technique) and that data must flow back to the incident record. Requirement on the platform.

**Operational context.**

- External Request (a request originating outside LSV, distinct from the External Agency > Request for Assistance Type)
- Off-duty response
- Multi-agency
- Extrication
- Mass Rescue (scale tag on a Rescue or SAR)

**Vessel Incident modifiers.**

- Injury / No Injury

**Dangerous Animal modifiers.**

- Confirmed / Reported
- Confirmation source (Lifeguard, Aerial, Member of public, External agency)

## Platform dev notes

Design constraints the platform must support.

**Required documentation rules.**

- Set required documents against an Incident Type. Inputs can include People (for example, patient count).
- Set required documents against Incident Tags.
- Distinguish between "form submission required" and "specific section within a form required".

**Tag scoping.**

- Constrain Tags to specific Incident Types by inclusion or exclusion. A Tag that only makes sense for Medical should not appear on a Marine Incident.

**Type states, platform behaviour.**

- Types are Abstract, Not Final, or Final. See Type states above.
- Abstract Types cannot be selected on open or close.
- Not Final Types can be opened but not closed. The user is prompted to refine before Finalising.
- Final Types can be opened and closed.

## Backwards compatibility

Every current category and type maps to exactly one new home: a Type, a Tag, an Agency Status, an Incident Outcome, or a linked-record concept. Nothing is lost.

Category-level map:

- SAR → Search And Rescue > Search or Rescue, refined to Final child.
- MED → Medical (Not Final), refined to an MPDS-aligned Final child before closure.
- VINC → Marine Incident > Vessel Incident > Assist or Report. Injury moves to Outcome and Tag.
- RESC → Search And Rescue > Rescue. Injury or no injury moves out of the Type onto the linked FAL.
- SHARK → Marine Incident > Dangerous Animal > Shark. Confirmation and source as Tags.
- DUR → Search And Rescue > Emergency > Duress Activation. Accidental as a Tag.
- Rescue Equipment Activation → Search And Rescue > Emergency > Rescue Equipment Activation.
- TASK → External Agency > Tasking.
- BAU → splits across Advisory Information, External Agency, and out-of-scope admin.
- FA → Incident Outcome False Alarm, not a Type.
- INC → decomposes into the proper branches above.
- MR (Mass Rescue) → scale Tag on a Rescue or SAR.

The full per-type map, covering all 72 current types, is in the Migration Map.

## Still open

1. Confirm the top-level tree structure (SAR / Medical / External Agency / Marine Incident / Advisory Information).
2. Confirm the Abstract / Not Final / Final assignment on each node. Medical as Not Final in particular, and whether SAR and Marine Incident should also be Not Final for the early window when the specific nature is unknown.

# Incident Categorisation

## Problem

The current incident categorisation model uses a category and type structure that has grown to a point where it creates ambiguity rather than clarity. A single incident can reasonably be classified under multiple types. Operators make different choices in the same situation, which degrades data consistency and makes it harder to report on, learn from, or compare incidents. The distinction between what constitutes a type and what is really an attribute of the incident is unclear, leading to types that exist to capture information rather than to classify, and unclear practice across different operators.

## Proposed change

Replace the current flat category and type model with an inheritance-based approach. A type can be a parent of another type, creating a clear decision tree that guides the operator to a single correct classification.

As part of this, separate what is genuinely an incident type from what is an attribute (called a Tag in the model design). Attributes describe characteristics of the incident, for example a SUP was involved or envenomation occurred. Types classify the nature of the incident itself.

The outcome is fewer types overall, a clear path from general to specific, a clear process for how an incident record should evolve, and no scenario where an operator is choosing between two equally valid options. This should result in consistent categorisation regardless of operator or surrounding circumstances.

## Impact

- Consistent classification across operators, shifts, and states
- Cleaner data for reporting, trend analysis, and benchmarking
- Faster incident creation, as operators follow a decision tree rather than a long list
- A foundation for AI-driven features that rely on structured, predictable data

## Themes

Simplification and Cohesion.

## Scope notes

- This brief is project 1.1 specifically, but is closely linked to Simplified Incident Creation (prerequisite) and Incident Tags (extension).
- The incident labels work (1.8) is closely coupled, as moving descriptive metadata into labels is what keeps the type hierarchy clean. Worth deciding upfront whether categorisation and labels are designed together.

## Design questions and where they landed

The questions this brief opened with, and their current state. The Model Design in this pack carries the detail.

1. **Where is the line between a type and an attribute?** Proposed in full. A value is a Type only if it changes what the incident fundamentally is. Otherwise it is a Tag, a Status, an Outcome, or clinical detail. See Model Design, Separation of concerns.
2. **What does the type hierarchy look like?** Proposed in full. See Model Design, Top-level Type tree and Medical branch.
3. **How does an incident record evolve as more is learned?** Proposed in full. The Type is only updated to correct miscategorisation, never because the incident evolved. Evolution is carried by Agency Status, Incident Outcome, Tags, and the Incident Log. See Model Design, Definitions.
4. **How do we migrate without losing historical comparability?** Drafted. Every one of the 72 current types is mapped in the Migration Map. Flagged rows remain open.
5. **How does this interact with incident labels?** Proposed in full. Tags and the Incident Labels project (priority 1.8) are one effort. The full tag taxonomy is still to be drafted.
6. **What is the minimum set of types, and how do we resist adding more?** Proposed in full. The governing rule plus the Abstract / Not Final / Final states keep the tree small. Open to SME pressure-testing.

## Next steps

- Circulate for feedback with LIMSOC and EMCaR team.
- Stand up the Incident Categorisation and Flow SME group and circulate this pack for input.
- Capture decisions in the Decision Log as they are made.

# LIMSOC Incident Categorisation

Operational Change Proposal, v0.8, 2 August 2026

*LIMSOC-BRIEF-LSV-2026-001 | Season 2026-27 | Focus Area 1: Enhance Our Incident Management | Working draft, not yet SME-circulated*

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| brief_id | LIMSOC-BRIEF-LSV-2026-001 |
| project_ref | 1.1 New Incident Categorisation |
| focus_area | 1. Enhance Our Incident Management |
| season | 2026-27 |
| status | draft v0.8 |
| owner | Nicholas Wood |
| sme_group | Incident Categorisation and Flow |
| themes | Simplification, Cohesion |
| last_updated | 2026-08-02 |

## About this pack

This pack proposes a new incident categorisation model for LIMSOC, Life Saving Victoria's operational incident-management system, and maps every current incident type to the new model. Nothing in this pack is endorsed yet.

**How to read it.** Part 1 explains the problem we have today. Part 2 explains the proposed model, one concept at a time, and why each piece exists. Part 3 describes what will change for operators, duty officers, and our leadership. Part 4 covers what happens next and what we need from you. The annexes hold the working detail: the full migration map for all 72 current types, the decision log, and the platform notes.

Feedback to Nicholas Wood, State Lifesaving Communications Officer.

---

# Part 1: The case for change

## The problem

Ask two experienced operators what an incident type means and when it should change, and you will get two different answers. That is not their fault. It has never been written down. The incident type is currently trying to be everything to everyone: what happened, how serious it was, who was involved, how it ended, and who asked us to attend. A field that carries all of that classifies nothing reliably.

The result is that a single incident can reasonably be categorised several different ways, and in practice, it is:

- There is no guidance on when something is a Marine Incident versus a Vessel Incident, so the same capsize lands in different places on different shifts.
- With no better guidance, a large share of in-water work is generalised to Rescue (In Water), Condition Unknown, and the detail is lost.
- Recovered from Water and Resuscitation overlap with no rule between them. Today we cannot tell whether a resuscitation was a patient we came across on the beach or a person we pulled from the water. Those are profoundly different stories, and our data cannot separate them.
- We cannot distinguish between assisting another agency to do their job and delivering our own service with other agencies alongside. Both look the same in the data.
- There is no rule for when an incident type should be updated, so sometimes it is and sometimes it is not, based on each individual's experience and view of what should happen. When a rescue becomes a drowning, the type is often overwritten, and the rescue disappears from the record. We cannot search for our Major Rescues, because some of them are no longer typed as rescues.
- The same confusion exists between records: there is no clear rule for when something is an incident, a rescue log, or a first aid form, so it is done inconsistently, and our statistics inherit that inconsistency.

Every one of these problems flows from the same root cause: none of these fields has a written definition, so each has drifted into whatever each operator understood it to be.

**What it costs us.** Every season, the EMCaR team pulls incident data for SLSA, for councils, for LSV, and for our own clubs and services. Because the data cannot be trusted at face value, each pull means manual interrogation and cleanup before anyone will stand behind the numbers. The effort is large, it repeats every season, and it caps what we can do: reporting we cannot produce, trends we cannot see, and questions we cannot answer.

## Why now

People have been saying for years that incident categorisation needs to be redone. It has not happened, because it is genuinely complex: 72 types, years of accumulated practice, and interagency dependencies. There is a lot of detail in this pack for the same reason. But the solution underneath it is simple, and once the core idea lands, everything else follows from it.

Two things make this the right moment:

**Our role has changed.** LSV Comms once spent its time signing on every unit. Digital advances in LIMSOC have retired that work. The principal job of LSV Comms now is to get the data right: to capture what actually happened in an incident, accurately and consistently. This proposal is that job.

**We have done this before.** Last season we replaced a rudimentary first aid form that was not fit for purpose. The old form asked a small set of basic questions that often did not match what had happened, and gave members no way to record the details that mattered. The new form asks questions based on what occurred: tick that oxygen was used, and the oxygen questions appear. The result was visibility we had never had. For the first time we could drill into the data and trust what it told us: which first aids are trending, where forms are being filled out incorrectly, and what is actually happening on our beaches. This proposal extends that same transformation from first aid to our entire incident response.

One more thing should be said plainly: this is a change, and change costs effort. But the current structure is already broken. Every season we run it, we accumulate more inconsistent data. Done well, we cannot get worse than we are today. We can only get better.

---

# Part 2: The proposal

## One idea: every value answers exactly one question

The whole model reduces to one principle. Every value attached to an incident answers exactly one question, and no two mechanisms answer the same question. This removes the ambiguity, streamlines the flow for members, and eliminates the duplication that degrades our data today. It simplifies our world: users' lives get easier, and the result gets better.

For the first time, each mechanism gets a written definition:

| Question | Mechanism | Cardinality | Example |
|----------|-----------|-------------|---------|
| What is it, fundamentally | Type (inheritance tree) | one | SAR, Rescue, Person |
| What qualifies or characterises it | Tags (the Incident Labels work, priority 1.8) | many | Resuscitation, Rescue Completed, External Request |
| Where is it in the lifecycle | Agency Status | one at a time | Responding, On Scene, Under Control |
| How did it end | Incident Outcome | one, gated by Type | Resolved, False Alarm, Fatality, Located |
| Assistance provided to one individual | Action Log (proposed merge of first aid form and rescue log, see below) | one per person helped | rescue, resus, fracture, marine sting |
| Part of a bigger event | Event | one | Wye River Floods |
| Free-form situational context | Incident Log | append-only | narrative entries with author and time |
| Free-form summary | Incident Name and Incident Brief | one each | short human-readable identifiers |

**Governing rule.** A value only earns its place as a Type if it changes what the incident fundamentally is. Otherwise it is a Tag, a Status, an Outcome, or Action Log detail.

Two definitions anchor everything else:

**Incident.** A response by Life Saving Victoria members that either:

- Requires a response from multiple lifesaving services, or
- Requires assistance from other emergency services, including all situations where there is a danger to human life, or
- Is otherwise serious or complex such that members would like support, assistance, and visibility from LSV Command.

**Event.** A major occurrence that results in, or has the potential to result in, multiple Incidents. An Event is the vehicle for associating multiple Incidents that share a common cause or context. Not all incidents will require an event association. Example: Wye River Floods.

## The fields around the Type

Before the type tree itself, the supporting fields. Each exists to take a job off the Type, so the Type can do one job well.

### Agency Status: where we are

Captures our overall status as an agency across the life of the incident:

1. Collecting Information
2. Responding
3. On Scene
4. Under Control
5. Returning
6. Finalising
7. Information Only (monitoring, aware but no active response)

Agency Status also carries the advisory-versus-response distinction: Information Only covers the advisory posture, and every other status is a response. This is why the model adopts no priority codes. MPDS surfaces ProQA determinant codes (Delta, Charlie, Bravo, Alpha, Omega), but for lifesaving we are either responding or it is advisory, and the status already says which. A priority field would duplicate information the model already holds.

### Incident Outcome: how it ended

A required selection when closing an incident. Controlled and mutually exclusive, with the options gated by Type:

- A Search surfaces: Located, Fatality, Stood Down.
- A Medical surfaces: Resolved, Referred to Agency, Fatality.
- A Rescue Equipment Activation surfaces the same outcomes as a Rescue, plus False Alarm.

The payoff is searchability. Today, when a rescue ends in a drowning, the type gets overwritten and the rescue vanishes from our statistics. With Outcome as its own field, we keep both truths: it was a Rescue, and it ended in a Fatality. We can finally search on each independently.

### Tags: what characterised it

Tags characterise. They never classify. An incident carries as many as apply. Draft groups:

**Care and clinical (form triggers).** Resuscitation, Member Injury, Penthrane Administered, Major First Aid, Oxygen Administered (each requiring an Action Log entry), and Rescue Completed (requiring the rescue detail, including method such as Heli rescue technique, which must flow back to the incident record: a platform requirement).

**Operational context.** External Request (a request originating outside LSV, distinct from the External Agency > Request for Assistance Type), Off-duty response, Multi-agency, Extrication, Mass Rescue (a scale tag on a Rescue or SAR).

**Vessel Incident modifiers.** Injury / No Injury.

**Dangerous Animal modifiers.** Confirmed / Reported, and Confirmation source (Lifeguard, Aerial, Member of public, External agency).

The full tag taxonomy is being drafted with the Incident Labels project (priority 1.8); the two are one effort.

### Incident Log, Name, and Brief

The Incident Log is the append-only narrative: timestamped entries with an author, carrying the situational context that does not belong in structured fields. Incident Name and Incident Brief remain the short human-readable identifiers.

## A new kind of Type

With every other question answered by a purpose-built field, the Type is free to answer just one: **what is the nature of the situation we are responding to?** The Type reflects the primary driver of the response, not everything that happens during it. A rescue followed by first aid is still a Rescue. A member of the public presenting on the beach with a major first aid is a Medical incident.

The structural change is to replace the current flat category-and-type list with an inheritance tree. A type can be the parent of another type, so classification becomes a walk from general to specific, and the operator is guided to a single correct answer instead of choosing from a list of 72. Fewer types overall, one clear home for every situation, and no scenario where two options are equally valid.

## Type states and guided questions

Two mechanisms make the tree work in practice.

**Type states.** Every node in the tree carries a state that governs when it can be used:

| State | Can open as this? | Can close as this? | Purpose |
|-------|-------------------|--------------------|---------|
| **Abstract** | No | No | Grouping node only. Structure and reporting, not selection. |
| **Not Final** | Yes | No | Can be opened while the specific nature is unknown. Must be refined to a Final child before closure. |
| **Final** | Yes | Yes | Fully specific. Terminal in the tree. |

For example, Medical is Not Final: an incident can be opened as Medical while the presenting problem is still being assessed, but before closure it must be refined to Chest Pain, Breathing Problems, and so on. Search and Rescue is Abstract: a bare SAR cannot be opened, one of its children must be selected. Chest Pain is Final.

This is also what retires the catch-all types (Other Incident, Other Medical, Other Vessel Incident). Instead of dumping the unknown into an "Other" bucket that tells us nothing, operators open at the most specific node they know, and refine before closure. Open wide, close narrow.

**Guided questions.** A Type may carry key questions, in the style of ProQA (the scripted question flow used by MPDS dispatch systems). Each answer does one of two things: drills to a child Type, or sets a controlled Tag. No per-incident custom fields are created; the questions populate the existing primitives. Questions are centrally defined per Type, and an answer never maps to free text that fragments data. A deliberately small set of true structured fields is kept only where the value is quantitative and reporting-critical (for example, number of people involved). Everything else defaults to Tags.

Specificity comes from the tree walk and the questions, not from a long type list.

## The rules that keep the data consistent

Four rules govern classification. Each one closes a specific gap that corrupts our data today.

### Rule 1: The Type is what we responded to

- The Type is updated only when new information clarifies that the initial classification was incorrect.
- The Type is never updated because the incident evolved.
- Evolution is captured in the Agency Status, the Incident Outcome, Tags, and the Incident Log.

This is the rule that fixes the disappearing Major Rescue. The rescue that becomes a drowning stays a Rescue, with Outcome: Fatality. It aligns with Ambulance Victoria practice, which does not recategorise unless the incident was misreported. And because the rule is written down, "sometimes updated, sometimes not" ends: no more individual judgment calls producing inconsistent records.

### Rule 2: One Type per incident

The Type captures the primary operational driver. Where two drivers genuinely co-occur, precedence selects the Type:

1. Search and Rescue or Rescue (a save wins)
2. Marine Incident
3. Medical
4. Advisory Information

Supporting principles: human first, vessel second (where a situation involves both people and a vessel, the Type follows the people); clinical detail always rides in the Action Log, never as a competing Type; and multiple separate responses to one situation group under an Event, they are not merged into one incident.

**Worked scenarios.**

1. **Rescue then major medical.** Swimmer pulled from a rip, arrests on the beach. Type is Rescue. Resuscitation rides as a Tag (Action Log required) and in the Action Log detail.
2. **Vessel incident producing a rescue.** Capsized vessel, people retrieved. Type is Rescue. Human first, vessel second. The vessel dimension is Tags and log.
3. **Medical during an External Agency Tasking.** Severity decides. A severe injury becomes its own linked incident. A minor one stays on the Tasking incident with a Member Injury Tag.
4. **Activation that becomes a rescue.** Stays one incident, typed as the activation. See Rule 4.

### Rule 3: Our incident or theirs

Whether something is a Tasking or our own incident is determined by our response. Are we delivering our services independently (including as part of an interagency response)? Then we open an incident of the appropriate type. Are we assisting another agency to perform their duties? Then it is External Agency > Tasking. This closes today's gap where the two are indistinguishable in the data.

**Worked example.** AV asks us to help carry their patient off the beach. We are a resource on AV's job: External Agency > Tasking, with tags and log notes as required. If instead we are managing the patient and called AV, it is Medical, with AV listed in responding services.

Extrication is an action, so it is a Tag, never a Type. This retires Assist Extrication as a Type.

### Rule 4: Activations keep their Type

When a Rescue Equipment Activation or Duress Activation leads to a real rescue, the incident stays as the activation Type it was opened as. One incident, no reclassification, no second incident. The rescue that follows is carried in Agency Status, Tags, Incident Outcome, and the log.

## The Action Log

*New in v0.8. Proposed here as a concept; detail to follow as its own piece of work.*

Today we run two per-person records, the first aid form and the rescue log, with no clear rule for when each applies. A person pulled from the water and treated on the beach might generate one, both, or neither, depending on who is filling it out. Members enter the same person's details twice when both apply. The inconsistency flows straight into our rescue and first aid statistics.

The proposal: merge them into one **Action Log**, defined as the assistance we provide to one individual. That assistance may be a rescue, a first aid, or both. The expectation becomes simple enough to say in one sentence: **one Action Log for each person we help, every time.** The person's details are entered once. Where the situation meets the criteria for an incident, the Action Logs are linked to that incident, exactly as first aid records link today.

This gives the guided-questions machinery a natural home on the per-person record too: the adaptive first aid form we already built becomes a section of the Action Log, appearing when care was provided, alongside rescue detail that appears when a rescue was performed.

Platform implications are noted in Annex C. This proposal supersedes the earlier First Aid Log (FAL) terminology decision, noted in the Decision Log.

## What this makes possible

Consistent, well-defined data is not the end goal. It is the foundation.

- **Backwards compatibility comes built in.** Every one of the 72 current types maps to exactly one home in the new model: a Type, a Tag, an Outcome, a Status, or a linked-record concept. Nothing is lost, and historical data stays comparable. The full map is Annex A.
- **Guided questions get smarter over time.** Centrally governed question flows can grow per Type without adding types or fields.
- **AI-enabled features become possible.** Structured, predictable data is the prerequisite for the features we want next: guided incident creation, quality checks at point of entry, automated summaries.
- **Expectations can rise naturally.** With clear definitions and a simpler flow, we can ask more of our members, because for the first time the system makes the right way the easy way.

# Part 3: What you will see

**Operators** get a guided path instead of a 72-item list, and a written definition for every field. The system asks the questions; the operator answers what they know. Faster incident creation, less second-guessing, and no more choosing between two equally defensible types at 2am.

**Duty officers and command** get a consistent common operating picture. The same situation looks the same regardless of who entered it or which shift entered it. Status, type, and outcome each mean one thing, so the picture reads at a glance.

**Our leadership and our services** get reporting that can finally be relied on. Season data for SLSA, councils, LSV, and our clubs stops being a manual interrogation exercise for the EMCaR team and becomes a query. Trends become visible. Questions get answered from the data instead of around it. That reliability compounds into everything the data touches: how we structure our services, how we support our members, and how we make the case for funding.

Together with the first aid form work, this presents a cohesive picture of operational data done properly, a piece of work LSV can be proud of and share with the other states as industry-leading.

## About this pack

This pack proposes a new incident categorisation model for LIMSOC, Life Saving Victoria's operational incident-management system, and maps every current incident type to the new model. Nothing in this pack is endorsed yet.

**How to read it.** Part 1 explains the problem we have today. Part 2 explains the proposed model, one concept at a time, and why each piece exists. Part 3 describes what will change for operators, duty officers, and our leadership. Part 4 covers what happens next and what we need from you. The annexes hold the working detail: the full migration map for all 72 current types, the decision log, and the platform notes.

Feedback to Nicholas Wood, State Lifesaving Communications Officer.

---

# Part 1: The case for change

## The problem

Ask two experienced operators what an incident type means and when it should change, and you will get two different answers. That is not their fault. It has never been written down. The incident type is currently trying to be everything to everyone: what happened, how serious it was, who was involved, how it ended, and who asked us to attend. A field that carries all of that classifies nothing reliably.

The result is that a single incident can reasonably be categorised several different ways, and in practice, it is:

- There is no guidance on when something is a Marine Incident versus a Vessel Incident, so the same capsize lands in different places on different shifts.
- With no better guidance, a large share of in-water work is generalised to Rescue (In Water), Condition Unknown, and the detail is lost.
- Recovered from Water and Resuscitation overlap with no rule between them. Today we cannot tell whether a resuscitation was a patient we came across on the beach or a person we pulled from the water. Those are profoundly different stories, and our data cannot separate them.
- We cannot distinguish between assisting another agency to do their job and delivering our own service with other agencies alongside. Both look the same in the data.
- There is no rule for when an incident type should be updated, so sometimes it is and sometimes it is not, based on each individual's experience and view of what should happen. When a rescue becomes a drowning, the type is often overwritten, and the rescue disappears from the record. We cannot search for our Major Rescues, because some of them are no longer typed as rescues.
- The same confusion exists between records: there is no clear rule for when something is an incident, a rescue log, or a first aid form, so it is done inconsistently, and our statistics inherit that inconsistency.

Every one of these problems flows from the same root cause: none of these fields has a written definition, so each has drifted into whatever each operator understood it to be.

**What it costs us.** Every season, the EMCaR team pulls incident data for SLSA, for councils, for LSV, and for our own clubs and services. Because the data cannot be trusted at face value, each pull means manual interrogation and cleanup before anyone will stand behind the numbers. The effort is large, it repeats every season, and it caps what we can do: reporting we cannot produce, trends we cannot see, and questions we cannot answer.

## Why now

People have been saying for years that incident categorisation needs to be redone. It has not happened, because it is genuinely complex: 72 types, years of accumulated practice, and interagency dependencies. There is a lot of detail in this pack for the same reason. But the solution underneath it is simple, and once the core idea lands, everything else follows from it.

Two things make this the right moment:

**Our role has changed.** LSV Comms once spent its time signing on every unit. Digital advances in LIMSOC have retired that work. The principal job of LSV Comms now is to get the data right: to capture what actually happened in an incident, accurately and consistently. This proposal is that job.

**We have done this before.** Last season we replaced a rudimentary first aid form that was not fit for purpose. The old form asked a small set of basic questions that often did not match what had happened, and gave members no way to record the details that mattered. The new form asks questions based on what occurred: tick that oxygen was used, and the oxygen questions appear. The result was visibility we had never had. For the first time we could drill into the data and trust what it told us: which first aids are trending, where forms are being filled out incorrectly, and what is actually happening on our beaches. This proposal extends that same transformation from first aid to our entire incident response.

One more thing should be said plainly: this is a change, and change costs effort. But the current structure is already broken. Every season we run it, we accumulate more inconsistent data. Done well, we cannot get worse than we are today. We can only get better.

---

# Part 2: The proposal

## One idea: every value answers exactly one question

The whole model reduces to one principle. Every value attached to an incident answers exactly one question, and no two mechanisms answer the same question. This removes the ambiguity, streamlines the flow for members, and eliminates the duplication that degrades our data today. It simplifies our world: users' lives get easier, and the result gets better.

For the first time, each mechanism gets a written definition:

| Question | Mechanism | Cardinality | Example |
|----------|-----------|-------------|---------|
| What is it, fundamentally | Type (inheritance tree) | one | SAR, Rescue, Person |
| What qualifies or characterises it | Tags (the Incident Labels work, priority 1.8) | many | Resuscitation, Rescue Completed, External Request |
| Where is it in the lifecycle | Agency Status | one at a time | Responding, On Scene, Under Control |
| How did it end | Incident Outcome | one, gated by Type | Resolved, False Alarm, Fatality, Located |
| Assistance provided to one individual | Action Log (proposed merge of first aid form and rescue log, see below) | one per person helped | rescue, resus, fracture, marine sting |
| Part of a bigger event | Event | one | Wye River Floods |
| Free-form situational context | Incident Log | append-only | narrative entries with author and time |
| Free-form summary | Incident Name and Incident Brief | one each | short human-readable identifiers |

**Governing rule.** A value only earns its place as a Type if it changes what the incident fundamentally is. Otherwise it is a Tag, a Status, an Outcome, or Action Log detail.

Two definitions anchor everything else:

**Incident.** A response by Life Saving Victoria members that either:

- Requires a response from multiple lifesaving services, or
- Requires assistance from other emergency services, including all situations where there is a danger to human life, or
- Is otherwise serious or complex such that members would like support, assistance, and visibility from LSV Command.

**Event.** A major occurrence that results in, or has the potential to result in, multiple Incidents. An Event is the vehicle for associating multiple Incidents that share a common cause or context. Not all incidents will require an event association. Example: Wye River Floods.

## The fields around the Type

Before the type tree itself, the supporting fields. Each exists to take a job off the Type, so the Type can do one job well.

### Agency Status: where we are

Captures our overall status as an agency across the life of the incident:

1. Collecting Information
2. Responding
3. On Scene
4. Under Control
5. Returning
6. Finalising
7. Information Only (monitoring, aware but no active response)

Agency Status also carries the advisory-versus-response distinction: Information Only covers the advisory posture, and every other status is a response. This is why the model adopts no priority codes. MPDS surfaces ProQA determinant codes (Delta, Charlie, Bravo, Alpha, Omega), but for lifesaving we are either responding or it is advisory, and the status already says which. A priority field would duplicate information the model already holds.

### Incident Outcome: how it ended

A required selection when closing an incident. Controlled and mutually exclusive, with the options gated by Type:

- A Search surfaces: Located, Fatality, Stood Down.
- A Medical surfaces: Resolved, Referred to Agency, Fatality.
- A Rescue Equipment Activation surfaces the same outcomes as a Rescue, plus False Alarm.

The payoff is searchability. Today, when a rescue ends in a drowning, the type gets overwritten and the rescue vanishes from our statistics. With Outcome as its own field, we keep both truths: it was a Rescue, and it ended in a Fatality. We can finally search on each independently.

### Tags: what characterised it

Tags characterise. They never classify. An incident carries as many as apply. Draft groups:

**Care and clinical (form triggers).** Resuscitation, Member Injury, Penthrane Administered, Major First Aid, Oxygen Administered (each requiring an Action Log entry), and Rescue Completed (requiring the rescue detail, including method such as Heli rescue technique, which must flow back to the incident record: a platform requirement).

**Operational context.** External Request (a request originating outside LSV, distinct from the External Agency > Request for Assistance Type), Off-duty response, Multi-agency, Extrication, Mass Rescue (a scale tag on a Rescue or SAR).

**Vessel Incident modifiers.** Injury / No Injury.

**Dangerous Animal modifiers.** Confirmed / Reported, and Confirmation source (Lifeguard, Aerial, Member of public, External agency).

The full tag taxonomy is being drafted with the Incident Labels project (priority 1.8); the two are one effort.

### Incident Log, Name, and Brief

The Incident Log is the append-only narrative: timestamped entries with an author, carrying the situational context that does not belong in structured fields. Incident Name and Incident Brief remain the short human-readable identifiers.

## A new kind of Type

With every other question answered by a purpose-built field, the Type is free to answer just one: **what is the nature of the situation we are responding to?** The Type reflects the primary driver of the response, not everything that happens during it. A rescue followed by first aid is still a Rescue. A member of the public presenting on the beach with a major first aid is a Medical incident.

The structural change is to replace the current flat category-and-type list with an inheritance tree. A type can be the parent of another type, so classification becomes a walk from general to specific, and the operator is guided to a single correct answer instead of choosing from a list of 72. Fewer types overall, one clear home for every situation, and no scenario where two options are equally valid.

## Type states and guided questions

Two mechanisms make the tree work in practice.

**Type states.** Every node in the tree carries a state that governs when it can be used:

| State | Can open as this? | Can close as this? | Purpose |
|-------|-------------------|--------------------|---------|
| **Abstract** | No | No | Grouping node only. Structure and reporting, not selection. |
| **Not Final** | Yes | No | Can be opened while the specific nature is unknown. Must be refined to a Final child before closure. |
| **Final** | Yes | Yes | Fully specific. Terminal in the tree. |

For example, Medical is Not Final: an incident can be opened as Medical while the presenting problem is still being assessed, but before closure it must be refined to Chest Pain, Breathing Problems, and so on. Search and Rescue is Abstract: a bare SAR cannot be opened, one of its children must be selected. Chest Pain is Final.

This is also what retires the catch-all types (Other Incident, Other Medical, Other Vessel Incident). Instead of dumping the unknown into an "Other" bucket that tells us nothing, operators open at the most specific node they know, and refine before closure. Open wide, close narrow.

**Guided questions.** A Type may carry key questions, in the style of ProQA (the scripted question flow used by MPDS dispatch systems). Each answer does one of two things: drills to a child Type, or sets a controlled Tag. No per-incident custom fields are created; the questions populate the existing primitives. Questions are centrally defined per Type, and an answer never maps to free text that fragments data. A deliberately small set of true structured fields is kept only where the value is quantitative and reporting-critical (for example, number of people involved). Everything else defaults to Tags.

Specificity comes from the tree walk and the questions, not from a long type list.

## The types

With the concepts in place, the tree itself:

- **Search And Rescue** [Abstract]
    - **Search** [Abstract]
        - Person [Not Final]
            - Land [Final]
            - Water [Final]
        - Vessel [Final]
    - **Rescue** [Abstract]
        - Person [Not Final]
            - Land [Final]
            - Water [Final]
        - Vessel [Final]
    - **Emergency** [Abstract]
        - Rescue Equipment Activation [Final]
        - Duress Activation [Final]
        - Flare Sighting [Final]
- **Welfare Check** [placement and state to be confirmed, see Part 4]
- **Medical** [Not Final]
    - MPDS-aligned children, see the Medical branch below.
- **External Agency** [Abstract]
    - Tasking [Final]
    - Request for Assistance [Final]
- **Marine Incident** [Abstract]
    - **Vessel Incident** [Abstract]
        - Assist [Final]
        - Report [Final]
    - **Dangerous Animal** [Abstract]
        - Shark [Final]
        - Other [Final]
- **Advisory Information** [Abstract]
    - Dangerous Conditions [Final]
    - Equipment Fault [Final]
    - Medication Discrepancy [Final]
    - Operational Change [Final]

**Out of scope for the incident taxonomy.** Administrative items (system status advisories, COVID-era system messaging) do not belong here. They move out of the incident taxonomy entirely.

### The Medical branch (MPDS-aligned)

Medical children align to the Medical Priority Dispatch System (MPDS) chief complaints, as used by Ambulance Victoria and maintained by the International Academies of Emergency Dispatch (IAED). MPDS is used here as a naming taxonomy for interagency alignment, not as a dispatch triage tool. When we hand over to AV, we are speaking the same language.

Medical is Not Final: every closed Medical incident must be refined to a Final child.

**Medical children (all Final).**

- Abdominal Pain / Problems
- Allergies (Reactions) / Envenomations (Stings, Bites). Marine envenomation rides here, animal identity as a Tag
- Animal Bites / Attacks
- Assault / Sexual Assault
- Back Pain (Non-Traumatic / Non-Recent)
- Breathing Problems
- Burns (Scalds) / Explosions
- Carbon Monoxide / Inhalation / HAZMAT / CBRN
- Cardiac or Respiratory Arrest / Death
- Chest Pain
- Choking
- Convulsions / Seizures
- Diabetic Problems
- Drowning / Diving / SCUBA Accident
- Electrocution / Lightning
- Eye Problems / Injuries
- Falls
- Headache
- Heat / Cold Exposure
- Hemorrhage / Lacerations
- Overdose / Poisoning (Ingestion)
- Stab / Gunshot / Penetrating Trauma
- Stroke (CVA) / Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)
- Traumatic Injuries
- Unconscious / Fainting (Near)
- Unknown Problem (Collapse, 3rd Party)

**Cut from the MPDS list, with reason.** Keeping the tree small is a design discipline: a chief complaint earns its place only if it is part of our operating context.

- Stun Gun component of the Assault compound: not our operating context.
- Pandemic / Epidemic / Outbreak (Surveillance or Triage): not the incident taxonomy. Sits in Advisory Information or system-level messaging if it ever needs a home.
- Inter-Facility Transfer / Palliative Care, and Inter-Facility Transfer for medically trained callers: patient transfer is not our operating context.
- Removed on review, 2026-07-09: Heart Problems / AICD, Inaccessible Incident / Entrapments, Pregnancy / Childbirth / Miscarriage, Psychiatric / Suicide Attempt, Sick Person, Traffic / Transportation Incidents, Automatic Crash Notification (ACN), HCP (Health-Care Practitioner) Referral.

**Worked example.** A bluebottle sting is Type: Medical > Allergies (Reactions) / Envenomations (Stings, Bites), Tag: Marine Envenomation, Tag: Bluebottle. Two stings with identical care pathways are one Type; the animal's identity characterises, it does not classify.

## The rules that keep the data consistent

Four rules govern classification. Each one closes a specific gap that corrupts our data today.

### Rule 1: The Type is what we responded to

- The Type is updated only when new information clarifies that the initial classification was incorrect.
- The Type is never updated because the incident evolved.
- Evolution is captured in the Agency Status, the Incident Outcome, Tags, and the Incident Log.

This is the rule that fixes the disappearing Major Rescue. The rescue that becomes a drowning stays a Rescue, with Outcome: Fatality. It aligns with Ambulance Victoria practice, which does not recategorise unless the incident was misreported. And because the rule is written down, "sometimes updated, sometimes not" ends: no more individual judgment calls producing inconsistent records.

### Rule 2: One Type per incident

The Type captures the primary operational driver. Where two drivers genuinely co-occur, precedence selects the Type:

1. Search and Rescue or Rescue (a save wins)
2. Marine Incident
3. Medical
4. Advisory Information

Supporting principles: human first, vessel second (where a situation involves both people and a vessel, the Type follows the people); clinical detail always rides in the Action Log, never as a competing Type; and multiple separate responses to one situation group under an Event, they are not merged into one incident.

**Worked scenarios.**

1. **Rescue then major medical.** Swimmer pulled from a rip, arrests on the beach. Type is Rescue. Resuscitation rides as a Tag (Action Log required) and in the Action Log detail.
2. **Vessel incident producing a rescue.** Capsized vessel, people retrieved. Type is Rescue. Human first, vessel second. The vessel dimension is Tags and log.
3. **Medical during an External Agency Tasking.** Severity decides. A severe injury becomes its own linked incident. A minor one stays on the Tasking incident with a Member Injury Tag.
4. **Activation that becomes a rescue.** Stays one incident, typed as the activation. See Rule 4.

### Rule 3: Our incident or theirs

Whether something is a Tasking or our own incident is determined by our response. Are we delivering our services independently (including as part of an interagency response)? Then we open an incident of the appropriate type. Are we assisting another agency to perform their duties? Then it is External Agency > Tasking. This closes today's gap where the two are indistinguishable in the data.

**Worked example.** AV asks us to help carry their patient off the beach. We are a resource on AV's job: External Agency > Tasking, with tags and log notes as required. If instead we are managing the patient and called AV, it is Medical, with AV listed in responding services.

Extrication is an action, so it is a Tag, never a Type. This retires Assist Extrication as a Type.

### Rule 4: Activations keep their Type

When a Rescue Equipment Activation or Duress Activation leads to a real rescue, the incident stays as the activation Type it was opened as. One incident, no reclassification, no second incident. The rescue that follows is carried in Agency Status, Tags, Incident Outcome, and the log.

## The Action Log

*New in v0.8. Proposed here as a concept; detail to follow as its own piece of work.*

Today we run two per-person records, the first aid form and the rescue log, with no clear rule for when each applies. A person pulled from the water and treated on the beach might generate one, both, or neither, depending on who is filling it out. Members enter the same person's details twice when both apply. The inconsistency flows straight into our rescue and first aid statistics.

The proposal: merge them into one **Action Log**, defined as the assistance we provide to one individual. That assistance may be a rescue, a first aid, or both. The expectation becomes simple enough to say in one sentence: **one Action Log for each person we help, every time.** The person's details are entered once. Where the situation meets the criteria for an incident, the Action Logs are linked to that incident, exactly as first aid records link today.

This gives the guided-questions machinery a natural home on the per-person record too: the adaptive first aid form we already built becomes a section of the Action Log, appearing when care was provided, alongside rescue detail that appears when a rescue was performed.

Platform implications are noted in Annex C. This proposal supersedes the earlier First Aid Log (FAL) terminology decision, noted in the Decision Log.

## What this makes possible

Consistent, well-defined data is not the end goal. It is the foundation.

- **Backwards compatibility comes built in.** Every one of the 72 current types maps to exactly one home in the new model: a Type, a Tag, an Outcome, a Status, or a linked-record concept. Nothing is lost, and historical data stays comparable. The full map is Annex A.
- **Guided questions get smarter over time.** Centrally governed question flows can grow per Type without adding types or fields.
- **AI-enabled features become possible.** Structured, predictable data is the prerequisite for the features we want next: guided incident creation, quality checks at point of entry, automated summaries.
- **Expectations can rise naturally.** With clear definitions and a simpler flow, we can ask more of our members, because for the first time the system makes the right way the easy way.

---

# Part 3: What you will see

**Operators** get a guided path instead of a 72-item list, and a written definition for every field. The system asks the questions; the operator answers what they know. Faster incident creation, less second-guessing, and no more choosing between two equally defensible types at 2am.

**Duty officers and command** get a consistent common operating picture. The same situation looks the same regardless of who entered it or which shift entered it. Status, type, and outcome each mean one thing, so the picture reads at a glance.

**Our leadership and our services** get reporting that can finally be relied on. Season data for SLSA, councils, LSV, and our clubs stops being a manual interrogation exercise for the EMCaR team and becomes a query. Trends become visible. Questions get answered from the data instead of around it. That reliability compounds into everything the data touches: how we structure our services, how we support our members, and how we make the case for funding.

Together with the first aid form work, this presents a cohesive picture of operational data done properly, a piece of work LSV can be proud of and share with the other states as industry-leading.

---

# Part 4: Next steps and what we need from you

**Process.** Stand up the Incident Categorisation and Flow SME group, circulate this pack, and capture decisions in the Decision Log (Annex B) as they are made, so settled points are not relitigated.

**What we need from you.**

- Review the model. In particular the top-level tree and the Abstract / Not Final / Final assignments.
- Give a view on the flagged Migration Map rows (Annex A).

1. Confirm the top-level tree structure (SAR / Welfare Check / Medical / External Agency / Marine Incident / Advisory Information).
2. Confirm the Abstract / Not Final / Final assignment on each node. Medical as Not Final in particular, and whether SAR and Marine Incident should also be Not Final for the early window when the specific nature is unknown.

5. Draft the full tag taxonomy with the Incident Labels project (1.8).
6. Detail the Action Log proposal as its own piece of work.

## Design questions and where they landed

The questions this work opened with, and their current state.

1. **Where is the line between a type and an attribute?** Proposed in full. A value is a Type only if it changes what the incident fundamentally is. Otherwise it is a Tag, a Status, an Outcome, or Action Log detail. See Part 2, One idea.
2. **What does the type hierarchy look like?** Proposed in full. See Part 2, The types.
3. **How does an incident record evolve as more is learned?** Proposed in full. The Type is only updated to correct miscategorisation, never because the incident evolved. Evolution is carried by Agency Status, Incident Outcome, Tags, and the Incident Log. See Part 2, Rule 1.
4. **How do we migrate without losing historical comparability?** Drafted. Every one of the 72 current types is mapped in Annex A. Flagged rows remain open.
5. **How does this interact with incident labels?** Proposed in full. Tags and the Incident Labels project (priority 1.8) are one effort. The full tag taxonomy is still to be drafted.
6. **What is the minimum set of types, and how do we resist adding more?** Proposed in full. The governing rule plus the Abstract / Not Final / Final states keep the tree small. Open to SME pressure-testing.

# Annex C: Platform dev notes

Design constraints the platform must support.

**Required documentation rules.**

- Set required documents against an Incident Type. Inputs can include People (for example, patient count).
- Set required documents against Incident Tags.
- Distinguish between "form submission required" and "specific section within a form required".

**Tag scoping.**

- Constrain Tags to specific Incident Types by inclusion or exclusion. A Tag that only makes sense for Medical should not appear on a Marine Incident.

**Type states, platform behaviour.**

- Types are Abstract, Not Final, or Final. See Part 2, Type states.
- Abstract Types cannot be selected on open or close.
- Not Final Types can be opened but not closed. The user is prompted to refine before finalising.
- Final Types can be opened and closed.

**Action Log (proposed).**

- A single per-person record replacing the first aid form and rescue log. One Action Log per individual assisted.
- Sections appear conditionally: care sections when treatment was provided (the adaptive first aid form becomes a section), rescue detail when a rescue was performed (method, including Heli technique, flowing back to the incident record).
- Action Logs link to an incident when the incident criteria are met, as first aid records link today.
- Existing form-trigger Tags (Resuscitation, Member Injury, Penthrane Administered, Major First Aid, Oxygen Administered, Rescue Completed) become Action Log requirements.

# DocxExport — markdown → .docx, formatting-faithful

Exports Nick's resumes and cover letters from markdown to `.docx` that match the
originals exactly: same font, sizes, ligatures, spacing, headings, bullets,
margins, header/footer. No more "the formatting came out too simple."

## How it works (template surgery)

A `.docx` is a zip of XML parts. Prior export attempts *regenerated* styling from
scratch (and got it wrong). This tool instead **keeps the original document as a
template and replaces only the body**:

- `word/styles.xml`, `theme1.xml`, `fontTable.xml`, `settings.xml` (ligatures),
  `numbering.xml`, headers/footers, `docProps`, theme — all preserved **byte for
  byte**.
- Only `word/document.xml` (the body text) and its `.rels` are regenerated.
- Every paragraph/run in the new body is built by **cloning the exact property
  blocks** captured from the template at runtime.

So fidelity is a *consequence* of reusing the originals, not something re-derived.
The cover-letter output is byte-identical to the original on every formatting
dimension; see `bun src/selftest.ts`.

## Usage

```bash
cd ~/.claude/PAI/TOOLS/DocxExport

# Cover letter
bun src/export.ts coverletter letter.md "out.docx"

# Resume
bun src/export.ts resume resume.md "out.docx"

# Use a different original as the style template (e.g. a specific historical CV)
bun src/export.ts resume resume.md out.docx --template "/path/to/Original.docx"
```

Write straight to OneDrive (exports only — never put `.md` in OneDrive):

```bash
bun src/export.ts coverletter letter.md \
  "$HOME/OneDrive/02_Career/Job_Applications/2026/<Company>/Cover Letter - Nicholas Wood.docx"
```

## Why now

input.old_string:
People have been saying for years that incident categorisation needs to be redone. It has not happened, because it is genuinely complex: 72 types, years of accumulated practice, and interagency dependencies. There is a lot of detail in this pack for the same reason. But the solution underneath it is simple, and once the core idea lands, everything else follows from it.

Two things make this the right moment:

**Our role has changed.** LSV Comms once spent its time signing on every unit. Digital advances in LIMSOC have retired that work. The principal job of LSV Comms now is to get the data right: to capture what actually happened in an incident, accurately and consistently. This proposal is that job.

**We have done this before.** Last season we replaced a rudimentary first aid form that was not fit for purpose. The old form asked a small set of basic questions that often did not match what had happened, and gave members no way to record the details that mattered. The new form asks questions based on what occurred: tick that oxygen was used, and the oxygen questions appear. The result was visibility we had never had. For the first time we could drill into the data and trust what it told us: which first aids are trending, where forms are being filled out incorrectly, and what is actually happening on our beaches. This proposal extends that same transformation from first aid to our entire incident response.

One more thing should be said plainly: this is a change, and change costs effort. But the current structure is already broken. Every season we run it, we accumulate more inconsistent data. Done well, we cannot get worse than we are today. We can only get better.
input.new_string:
The need to redesign incident categorisation has been recognised for years. It has not been done because the problem is genuinely complex: 72 types, years of accumulated practice, and interagency dependencies. The level of detail in this pack reflects that complexity. The underlying solution, however, is simple, and every element of the design follows from a single principle set out in Part 2.

**Guided questions.** A Type may carry key questions, in the style of ProQA (the scripted question flow used by MPDS dispatch systems). input.old_string:
Today we run two per-person records, the first aid form and the rescue log, with no clear rule for when each applies. A person pulled from the water and treated on the beach might generate one, both, or neither, depending on who is filling it out. Members enter the same person's details twice when both apply. The inconsistency flows straight into our rescue and first aid statistics.

The proposal: merge them into one **Action Log**, defined as the assistance we provide to one individual. That assistance may be a rescue, a first aid, or both. The expectation becomes simple enough to say in one sentence: **one Action Log for each person we help, every time.** The person's details are entered once. Today we maintain two per-person records, the first aid form and the rescue log, with no clear rule for when each applies. A person retrieved from the water and treated on the beach might generate one, both, or neither, depending on who completes the record. Members enter the same person's details twice when both apply. The inconsistency flows directly into our rescue and first aid statistics.

The proposal is to merge them into one **Action Log**, defined as the assistance we provide to one individual. That assistance may be a rescue, a first aid, or both. The expectation for members reduces to a single sentence: **one Action Log for each person assisted, every time.** The person's details are entered once. Where the situation meets the criteria for an incident, the Action Logs are linked to that incident, exactly as first aid records link today.
