19	## About this pack
20	
21	This pack proposes a new incident categorisation model for LIMSOC, Life Saving Victoria's operational incident-management system, and maps every current incident type to the new model. Nothing in this pack is endorsed yet.
22	
23	**How to read it.** Part 1 explains the problem we have today. Part 2 explains the proposed model, one concept at a time, and why each piece exists. Part 3 describes what will change for operators, duty officers, and our leadership. Part 4 covers what happens next and what we need from you. The annexes hold the working detail: the full migration map for all 72 current types, the decision log, and the platform notes.
24	
25	Feedback to Nicholas Wood, State Lifesaving Communications Officer.
26	
27	---
28	
29	# Part 1: The case for change
30	
31	## The problem
32	
33	The current model provides no written definition of what an incident type represents or when it should be updated. In the absence of a definition, the type has been asked to carry every dimension of an incident: what happened, how serious it was, who was involved, how it ended, and who requested our attendance. A field that carries all of these dimensions cannot classify any of them reliably, and each operator's interpretation of it necessarily differs.
34	
35	As a result, a single incident can reasonably be categorised in several different ways, and in current practice it is:
36	
37	- There is no guidance on when something is a Marine Incident versus a Vessel Incident, so the same capsize is recorded differently on different shifts.
38	- With no better guidance, a large share of in-water work is generalised to Rescue (In Water), Condition Unknown, and the detail is lost.
39	- Recovered from Water and Resuscitation overlap with no rule between them. Today we cannot tell whether a resuscitation was a patient encountered on the beach or a person retrieved from the water. These are operationally distinct situations that the data cannot separate.
40	- We cannot distinguish between assisting another agency to do their job and delivering our own service with other agencies alongside. Both look the same in the data.
41	- There is no rule for when an incident type should be updated, so update practice varies with each individual's experience and view of what should happen. When a rescue becomes a drowning, the type is frequently overwritten and the rescue is lost from the record. Major Rescues cannot be reliably searched, because some are no longer typed as rescues.
42	- The same confusion exists between records: there is no clear rule for when something is an incident, a rescue log, or a first aid form, so it is done inconsistently, and our statistics inherit that inconsistency.
43	
44	These problems share a single root cause: no field in the current model carries a written definition, so practice on each has drifted into individual interpretation.
45	
46	**The cost.** Every season, the EMCaR team pulls incident data for SLSA, for councils, for LSV, and for our own clubs and services. Because the data cannot be taken at face value, each pull requires manual interrogation and correction before the figures can be relied upon. The effort is substantial, it recurs every season, and it limits what can be delivered: reporting that cannot be produced, trends that cannot be seen, and questions that cannot be answered.
47	
48	## Why now
49	
50	The need to redesign incident categorisation has been recognised for years. It has not been done because the problem is genuinely complex: 72 types, years of accumulated practice, and interagency dependencies. The level of detail in this pack reflects that complexity. The underlying solution, however, is simple, and every element of the design follows from a single principle set out in Part 2.
51	
52	Two developments make this the right time.
53	
54	**The role has changed.** LSV Comms once spent much of its effort signing on every unit. Digital advances in LIMSOC have removed that workload. The principal responsibility of LSV Comms is now data quality: capturing what happened in an incident accurately and consistently. This proposal is a direct exercise of that responsibility.
55	
56	**The approach is proven.** Last season the first aid form was rebuilt from a rudimentary form that was not fit for purpose. The previous form asked a small set of fixed questions that frequently did not match the situation and gave members no way to record the details that mattered. The replacement asks questions based on what occurred: where oxygen use is recorded, the oxygen questions are presented. The result was visibility that had not existed before. For the first time the data could be interrogated with confidence: which first aid presentations are trending, where forms are completed incorrectly, and what is occurring on our beaches. This proposal applies the same transformation to the incident record.
57	
58	The risk profile of the change should also be stated clearly. The current structure is already producing inconsistent data, and every season it operates adds to that inconsistency. The transition carries effort, but it carries no realistic risk of degrading data quality below its current state. It can only improve it.
59	
60	---
61	
62	# Part 2: The proposal
63	
64	## One idea: every value answers exactly one question
65	
66	The model rests on one principle. Every value attached to an incident answers exactly one question, and no two mechanisms answer the same question. This removes ambiguity, streamlines the workflow for members, and eliminates the duplication that degrades data quality today: a simpler model that is easier to use and produces a better result.
67	
68	Each mechanism is given a written definition, for the first time:
69	
70	| Question | Mechanism | Cardinality | Example |
71	|----------|-----------|-------------|---------|
72	| What is it, fundamentally | Type (inheritance tree) | one | SAR, Rescue, Person |
73	| What qualifies or characterises it | Tags (the Incident Labels work, priority 1.8) | many | Resuscitation, Rescue Completed, External Request |
74	| Where is it in the lifecycle | Agency Status | one at a time | Responding, On Scene, Under Control |
75	| How did it end | Incident Outcome | one, gated by Type | Resolved, False Alarm, Fatality, Located |
76	| Assistance provided to one individual | Action Log (proposed merge of first aid form and rescue log, see below) | one per person helped | rescue, resus, fracture, marine sting |
77	| Part of a bigger event | Event | one | Wye River Floods |
78	| Free-form situational context | Incident Log | append-only | narrative entries with author and time |
79	| Free-form summary | Incident Name and Incident Brief | one each | short human-readable identifiers |
80	
81	**Governing rule.** A value only earns its place as a Type if it changes what the incident fundamentally is. Otherwise it is a Tag, a Status, an Outcome, or Action Log detail.
82	
83	Two definitions anchor everything else:
84	
85	**Incident.** A response by Life Saving Victoria members that either:
86	
87	- Requires a response from multiple lifesaving services, or
88	- Requires assistance from other emergency services, including all situations where there is a danger to human life, or
89	- Is otherwise serious or complex such that members would like support, assistance, and visibility from LSV Command.

1	# LIMSOC Incident Categorisation
2	
3	Operational Change Proposal, v0.8.2, 3 August 2026
4	
5	*LIMSOC-BRIEF-LSV-2026-001 | Season 2026-27 | Focus Area 1: Enhance Our Incident Management | Working draft, not yet SME-circulated*
6	
7	| Field | Value |
8	|-------|-------|
9	| brief_id | LIMSOC-BRIEF-LSV-2026-001 |
10	| project_ref | 1.1 New Incident Categorisation |
11	| focus_area | 1. Enhance Our Incident Management |
12	| season | 2026-27 |
13	| status | draft v0.8.2 |
14	| owner | Nicholas Wood |
15	| sme_group | Incident Categorisation and Flow |
16	| themes | Simplification, Cohesion |
17	| last_updated | 2026-08-03 |
18	
19	## About this pack
20	
21	This pack proposes a new incident categorisation model for LIMSOC, Life Saving Victoria's operational incident-management system, and maps every current incident type to the new model. Nothing in this pack is endorsed yet.
22	
23	**How to read it.** Part 1 explains the problem we have today. Part 2 explains the proposed model, one concept at a time, and why each piece exists. Part 3 describes what will change for operators, duty officers, and our leadership. Part 4 covers what happens next and what we need from you. The annexes hold the working detail: the full migration map for all 72 current types, the decision log, and the platform notes.
24	
25	Feedback to Nicholas Wood, State Lifesaving Communications Officer.
26	
27	---
28	
29	# Part 1: The case for change
30	
31	## The problem
32	
33	The current model provides no written definition of what an incident type represents or when it should be updated. In the absence of a definition, the type has been asked to carry every dimension of an incident: what happened, how serious it was, who was involved, how it ended, and who requested our attendance. A field that carries all of these dimensions cannot classify any of them reliably, and each operator's interpretation of it necessarily differs.
34	
35	As a result, a single incident can reasonably be categorised in several different ways, and in current practice it is:
36	
37	- There is no guidance on when something is a Marine Incident versus a Vessel Incident, so the same capsize is recorded differently on different shifts.
38	- With no better guidance, a large share of in-water work is generalised to Rescue (In Water), Condition Unknown, and the detail is lost.
39	- Recovered from Water and Resuscitation overlap with no rule between them. Today we cannot tell whether a resuscitation was a patient encountered on the beach or a person retrieved from the water. These are operationally distinct situations that the data cannot separate.
40	- We cannot distinguish between assisting another agency to do their job and delivering our own service with other agencies alongside. Both look the same in the data.
41	- There is no rule for when an incident type should be updated, so update practice varies with each individual's experience and view of what should happen. When a rescue becomes a drowning, the type is frequently overwritten and the rescue is lost from the record. Major Rescues cannot be reliably searched, because some are no longer typed as rescues.
42	- The same confusion exists between records: there is no clear rule for when something is an incident, a rescue log, or a first aid form, so it is done inconsistently, and our statistics inherit that inconsistency.
43	
44	These problems share a single root cause: no field in the current model carries a written definition, so practice on each has drifted into individual interpretation.
45	
46	**The cost.** Every season, the EMCaR team pulls incident data for SLSA, for councils, for LSV, and for our own clubs and services. Because the data cannot be taken at face value, each pull requires manual interrogation and correction before the figures can be relied upon. The effort is substantial, it recurs every season, and it limits what can be delivered: reporting that cannot be produced, trends that cannot be seen, and questions that cannot be answered.
47	
48	## Why now
49	
50	The need to redesign incident categorisation has been recognised for years. It has not been done because the problem is genuinely complex: 72 types, years of accumulated practice, and interagency dependencies. The level of detail in this pack reflects that complexity. The underlying solution, however, is simple, and every element of the design follows from a single principle set out in Part 2.
51	
52	Two developments make this the right time.
53	
54	**The role has changed.** LSV Comms once spent much of its effort signing on every unit. Digital advances in LIMSOC have removed that workload. The principal responsibility of LSV Comms is now data quality: capturing what happened in an incident accurately and consistently. This proposal is a direct exercise of that responsibility.
55	
56	**The approach is proven.** Last season the first aid form was rebuilt from a rudimentary form that was not fit for purpose. The previous form asked a small set of fixed questions that frequently did not match the situation and gave members no way to record the details that mattered. The replacement asks questions based on what occurred: where oxygen use is recorded, the oxygen questions are presented. The result was visibility that had not existed before. For the first time the data could be interrogated with confidence: which first aid presentations are trending, where forms are completed incorrectly, and what is occurring on our beaches. This proposal applies the same transformation to the incident record.
57	
58	The risk profile of the change should also be stated clearly. The current structure is already producing inconsistent data, and every season it operates adds to that inconsistency. The transition carries effort, but it carries no realistic risk of degrading data quality below its current state. It can only improve it.
59	
60	---
61	
62	# Part 2: The proposal
63	
64	## One idea: every value answers exactly one question
65	
66	The model rests on one principle. Every value attached to an incident answers exactly one question, and no two mechanisms answer the same question. This removes ambiguity, streamlines the workflow for members, and eliminates the duplication that degrades data quality today: a simpler model that is easier to use and produces a better result.
67	
68	Each mechanism is given a written definition, for the first time:
69	
70	| Question | Mechanism | Cardinality | Example |
71	|----------|-----------|-------------|---------|
72	| What is it, fundamentally | Type (inheritance tree) | one | SAR, Rescue, Person |
73	| What qualifies or characterises it | Tags (the Incident Labels work, priority 1.8) | many | Resuscitation, Rescue Completed, External Request |
74	| Where is it in the lifecycle | Agency Status | one at a time | Responding, On Scene, Under Control |
75	| How did it end | Incident Outcome | one, gated by Type | Resolved, False Alarm, Fatality, Located |
76	| Assistance provided to one individual | Action Log (proposed merge of first aid form and rescue log, see below) | one per person helped | rescue, resus, fracture, marine sting |
77	| Part of a bigger event | Event | one | Wye River Floods |
78	| Free-form situational context | Incident Log | append-only | narrative entries with author and time |
79	| Free-form summary | Incident Name and Incident Brief | one each | short human-readable identifiers |
80	
81	**Governing rule.** A value only earns its place as a Type if it changes what the incident fundamentally is. Otherwise it is a Tag, a Status, an Outcome, or Action Log detail.
82	
83	Two definitions anchor everything else:
84	
85	**Incident.** A response by Life Saving Victoria members that either:
86	
87	- Requires a response from multiple lifesaving services, or
88	- Requires assistance from other emergency services, including all situations where there is a danger to human life, or
89	- Is otherwise serious or complex such that members would like support, assistance, and visibility from LSV Command.
90

In the absence of a definition, the type has been asked to carry every dimension of an incident: what happened, how serious it was, who was involved, how it ended, and who requested our attendance. A field that carries all of these dimensions cannot classify any of them reliably, and each operator's interpretation of it necessarily differs.

**The approach is proven.** Last season the first aid form was rebuilt from a rudimentary form that was not fit for purpose. The previous form asked a small set of fixed questions that frequently did not match the situation and gave members no way to record the details that mattered. The replacement asks questions based on what occurred: where oxygen use is recorded, the oxygen questions are presented. The result was visibility that had not existed before. For the first time the data could be interrogated with confidence: which first aid presentations are trending, where forms are completed incorrectly, and what is occurring on our beaches. This proposal applies the same transformation to the incident record.

lines: ## A new kind of Type

-With every other question answered by a purpose-built field, the Type answers only one: **the nature of the situation we are responding to.** The Type reflects the primary driver of the response, not everything that happens during it. A rescue followed by first aid is still a Rescue. A member of the public presenting on the beach with a major first aid is a Medical incident.

+With every other question answered by a purpose-built field, the Type answers only one question, **the nature of the situation we are responding to.** The Type reflects the primary driver of the response, not everything that happens during it. A rescue followed by first aid is still a Rescue. A member of the public presenting on the beach with a major first aid is a Medical incident.

The structural change is to replace the current flat category-and-type list with an inheritance tree. A type can be the parent of another type, so classification becomes a walk from general to specific, and the operator is guided to a single correct answer instead of choosing from a list of 72. Fewer types overall, one clear home for every situation, and no scenario where two options are equally valid.

35:As a result, a single incident can reasonably be categorised in several different ways, and in current practice it is:
42:- The same confusion exists between records: there is no clear rule for when something is an incident, a rescue log, or a first aid form, so it is done inconsistently, and our statistics inherit that inconsistency.
44:These problems share a single root cause: no field in the current model carries a written definition, so practice on each has drifted into individual interpretation.
46:**The cost.** Every season, the EMCaR team pulls incident data for SLSA, for councils, for LSV, and for our own clubs and services. Because the data cannot be taken at face value, each pull requires manual interrogation and correction before the figures can be relied upon. The effort is substantial, it recurs every season, and it limits what can be delivered: reporting that cannot be produced, trends that cannot be seen, and questions that cannot be answered.
68:Each mechanism is given a written definition, for the first time:
83:Two definitions anchor everything else:
85:**Incident.** A response by Life Saving Victoria members that either:
91:**Event.** A major occurrence that results in, or has the potential to result in, multiple Incidents. An Event is the vehicle for associating multiple Incidents that share a common cause or context. Not all incidents will require an event association. Example: Wye River Floods.
99:Captures our overall status as an agency across the life of the incident:
109:Agency Status also carries the advisory-versus-response distinction: Information Only covers the advisory posture, and every other status is a response. This is why the model adopts no priority codes. MPDS surfaces ProQA determinant codes (Delta, Charlie, Bravo, Alpha, Omega), but for lifesaving we are either responding or it is advisory, and the status already says which. A priority field would duplicate information the model already holds.
119:The benefit is searchability. Today, when a rescue ends in a drowning, the type is overwritten and the rescue is lost from our statistics. With Outcome as its own field, both facts are preserved: the incident was a Rescue, and it ended in a Fatality. Each can be searched independently.
123:Tags characterise. They never classify. An incident carries as many as apply. Draft groups:
125:**Care and clinical (form triggers).** Resuscitation, Member Injury, Penthrane Administered, Major First Aid, Oxygen Administered (each requiring an Action Log entry), and Rescue Completed (requiring the rescue detail, including method such as Heli rescue technique, which must flow back to the incident record: a platform requirement).
137:The Incident Log is the append-only narrative: timestamped entries with an author, carrying the situational context that does not belong in structured fields. Incident Name and Incident Brief remain the short human-readable identifiers.
149:**Type states.** Every node in the tree carries a state that governs when it can be used:
161:**Guided questions.** A Type may carry key questions, in the style of ProQA (the scripted question flow used by MPDS dispatch systems). Each answer does one of two things: drills to a child Type, or sets a controlled Tag. No per-incident custom fields are created; the questions populate the existing primitives. Questions are centrally defined per Type, and an answer never maps to free text that fragments data. A deliberately small set of true structured fields is kept only where the value is quantitative and reporting-critical (for example, number of people involved). Everything else defaults to Tags.
209:Medical is Not Final: every closed Medical incident must be refined to a Final child.
240:**Cut from the MPDS list, with reason.** Keeping the tree small is a design discipline: a chief complaint earns its place only if it is part of our operating context.
242:- Stun Gun component of the Assault compound: not our operating context.
243:- Pandemic / Epidemic / Outbreak (Surveillance or Triage): not the incident taxonomy. Sits in Advisory Information or system-level messaging if it ever needs a home.
244:- Inter-Facility Transfer / Palliative Care, and Inter-Facility Transfer for medically trained callers: patient transfer is not our operating context.
245:- Removed on review, 2026-07-09: Heart Problems / AICD, Inaccessible Incident / Entrapments, Pregnancy / Childbirth / Miscarriage, Psychiatric / Suicide Attempt, Sick Person, Traffic / Transportation Incidents, Automatic Crash Notification (ACN), HCP (Health-Care Practitioner) Referral.
270:Supporting principles: human first, vessel second (where a situation involves both people and a vessel, the Type follows the people); clinical detail always rides in the Action Log, never as a competing Type; and multiple separate responses to one situation group under an Event, they are not merged into one incident.
283:**Worked example.** AV asks us to help carry their patient off the beach. We are a resource on AV's job: External Agency > Tasking, with tags and log notes as required. If instead we are managing the patient and called AV, it is Medical, with AV listed in responding services.

2

4

18	
19	## About this pack
20	
21	This pack proposes a new incident categorisation model for LIMSOC, Life Saving Victoria's operational incident-management system, and maps every current incident type to the new model. Nothing in this pack is endorsed yet.
22	
23	**How to read it.** Part 1 explains the problem we have today. Part 2 explains the proposed model, one concept at a time, and why each piece exists. Part 3 describes what will change for operators, duty officers, and our leadership. Part 4 covers what happens next and what we need from you. The annexes hold the working detail, including the full migration map for all 72 current types, the decision log, and the platform notes.
24	
25	Feedback to Nicholas Wood, State Lifesaving Communications Officer.
26	
27	---
28	
29	# Part 1. The case for change
30	
31	## The problem
32	
33	The current model provides no written definition of what an incident type represents or when it should be updated. In the absence of a definition, the type has been asked to carry every dimension of an incident, including what happened, how serious it was, who was involved, how it ended, and who requested our attendance. A field that carries all of these dimensions cannot classify any of them reliably, and each operator's interpretation of it necessarily differs.
34	
35	As a result, a single incident can reasonably be categorised in several different ways, and in current practice it is:
36	
37	- There is no guidance on when something is a Marine Incident versus a Vessel Incident, so the same capsize is recorded differently on different shifts.
38	- With no better guidance, a large share of in-water work is generalised to Rescue (In Water), Condition Unknown, and the detail is lost.
39	- Recovered from Water and Resuscitation overlap with no rule between them. Today we cannot tell whether a resuscitation was a patient encountered on the beach or a person retrieved from the water.
40	- We cannot distinguish between assisting another agency to do their job and delivering our own service with other agencies alongside. Both look the same in the data.
41	- There is no rule for when an incident type should be updated, so update practice varies with each individual's experience and view of what should happen. When a rescue becomes a drowning, the type is frequently overwritten and the rescue is lost from the record. Major Rescues cannot be reliably searched, because some are no longer typed as rescues.
42	- The same confusion exists between records: there is no clear rule for when something is an incident, a rescue log, or a first aid form, so it is done inconsistently, and our statistics inherit that inconsistency.
43	
44	These problems share a single root cause: no field in the current model carries a written definition, so practice on each has drifted into individual interpretation.
45	
46	**The cost.** Every season, the EMCaR team pulls incident data for SLSA, for councils, for LSV, and for our own clubs and services. Because the data cannot be taken at face value, each pull requires manual interrogation and correction before the figures can be relied upon. The effort is substantial, it recurs every season, and it limits what can be delivered: reporting that cannot be produced, trends that cannot be seen, and questions that cannot be answered.
47	
48	## Why now
49	
50	The need to redesign incident categorisation has been recognised for years. It has not been done because the problem is complex. There are 72 types, years of accumulated practice, and various dependencies. The underlying solution, whilst detailed, is simple, and every element of the design follows from a single principle set out in Part 2.
51	
52	Two developments make this the right time.
53	
54	**The role has changed.** LSV Comms once spent much of its effort signing on every unit. Digital advances in LIMSOC have removed that workload. The principal responsibility of LSV Comms is now data quality, capturing what happened in an incident accurately and consistently. This proposal is a direct exercise of that responsibility.
55	
56	**The approach is proven.** Last season the first aid form was rebuilt from a rudimentary form that was not fit for purpose. The previous form asked a small set of fixed questions that frequently did not match the situation and gave members no way to record the details that mattered. The replacement asks questions based on what occurred. Where oxygen use is recorded, the oxygen questions are presented. The result was visibility that had not existed before. For the first time the data could be interrogated with confidence, showing which first aid presentations are trending, where forms are completed incorrectly, and what is occurring on our beaches. This proposal applies the same transformation to the incident record.
57	
58	The risk profile of the change should also be stated clearly. The current structure is already producing inconsistent data, and every season it operates adds to that inconsistency. The transition carries effort, but it carries no realistic risk of degrading data quality below its current state. It can only improve it.
59	
60	---
61	
62	# Part 2. The proposal
63	
64	## One idea
65	
66	The model rests on one principle. Every value attached to an incident answers exactly one question, and no two mechanisms answer the same question. This removes ambiguity, streamlines the workflow for members, and eliminates the duplication that degrades data quality today. The result is a simpler model that is easier to use and produces better data.
67	
68	Each mechanism is given a written definition, for the first time:
69	
70	| Question | Mechanism | Cardinality | Example |
71	|----------|-----------|-------------|---------|
72	| What is it, fundamentally | Type (inheritance tree) | one | SAR, Rescue, Person |
73	| What qualifies or characterises it | Tags (the Incident Labels work, priority 1.8) | many | Resuscitation, Rescue Completed, External Request |
74	| Where is it in the lifecycle | Agency Status | one at a time | Responding, On Scene, Under Control |
75	| How did it end | Incident Outcome | one, gated by Type | Resolved, False Alarm, Fatality, Located |
76	| Assistance provided to one individual | Action Log (proposed merge of first aid form and rescue log, see below) | one per person helped | rescue, resus, fracture, marine sting |
77	| Part of a bigger event | Event | one | Wye River Floods |
78	| Free-form situational context | Incident Log | append-only | narrative entries with author and time |
79	| Free-form summary | Incident Name and Incident Brief | one each | short human-readable identifiers |
80	
81	**Governing rule.** A value only earns its place as a Type if it changes what the incident fundamentally is. Otherwise it is a Tag, a Status, an Outcome, or Action Log detail.
82	
83	Two definitions anchor everything else:
84	
85	**Incident.** A response by Life Saving Victoria members that either:
86	
87	- Requires a response from multiple lifesaving services, or
88	- Requires assistance from other emergency services, including all situations where there is a danger to human life, or
89	- Is otherwise serious or complex such that members would like support, assistance, and visibility from LSV Command.
90	
91	**Event.** A major occurrence that results in, or has the potential to result in, multiple Incidents. An Event is the vehicle for associating multiple Incidents that share a common cause or context. Not all incidents will require an event association. Example: Wye River Floods.

lines: Today we maintain two per-person records, the first aid form and the rescue log, with no clear rule for when each applies. A person retrieved from the water and treated on the beach might generate one, both, or neither, depending on who completes the record. Members enter the same person's details twice when both apply. The inconsistency flows directly into our rescue and first aid statistics.

-The proposal is to merge them into one **Action Log**, defined as the assistance we provide to one individual. That assistance may be a rescue, a first aid, or both. The expectation for members reduces to a single sentence: **one Action Log for each person assisted, every time.** The person's details are entered once. Where the situation meets the criteria for an incident, the Action Logs are linked to that incident, exactly as first aid records link today.

1	# LIMSOC Incident Categorisation
2	
3	Operational Change Proposal, v0.8.3, 3 August 2026
4	
5	*LIMSOC-BRIEF-LSV-2026-001 | Season 2026-27 | Focus Area 1: Enhance Our Incident Management | Working draft, not yet SME-circulated*
6	
7	| Field | Value |
8	|-------|-------|
9	| brief_id | LIMSOC-BRIEF-LSV-2026-001 |
10	| project_ref | 1.1 New Incident Categorisation |
11	| focus_area | 1. Enhance Our Incident Management |
12	| season | 2026-27 |
13	| status | draft v0.8.3 |
14	| owner | Nicholas Wood |
15	| sme_group | Incident Categorisation and Flow |
16	| themes | Simplification, Cohesion |
17	| last_updated | 2026-08-03 |
18	
19	## About this pack
20	
21	This pack proposes a new incident categorisation model for LIMSOC, Life Saving Victoria's operational incident-management system, and maps every current incident type to the new model. Nothing in this pack is endorsed yet.
22	
23	**How to read it.** Part 1 explains the problem we have today. Part 2 explains the proposed model, one concept at a time, and why each piece exists. Part 3 describes what will change for operators, duty officers, and our leadership. Part 4 covers what happens next and what we need from you. The annexes hold the working detail, including the full migration map for all 72 current types, the decision log, and the platform notes.
24	
25	Feedback to Nicholas Wood, State Lifesaving Communications Officer.
26	
27	---
28	
29	# Part 1. The case for change
30	
31	## The problem
32	
33	The current model provides no written definition of what an incident type represents or when it should be updated. In the absence of a definition, the type has been asked to carry every dimension of an incident, including what happened, how serious it was, who was involved, how it ended, and who requested our attendance. A field that carries all of these dimensions cannot classify any of them reliably, and each operator's interpretation of it necessarily differs.
34	
35	As a result, a single incident can reasonably be categorised in several different ways, and in current practice it is:
36	
37	- There is no guidance on when something is a Marine Incident versus a Vessel Incident, so the same capsize is recorded differently on different shifts.
38	- With no better guidance, a large share of in-water work is generalised to Rescue (In Water), Condition Unknown, and the detail is lost.
39	- Recovered from Water and Resuscitation overlap with no rule between them. Today we cannot tell whether a resuscitation was a patient encountered on the beach or a person retrieved from the water.
40	- We cannot distinguish between assisting another agency to do their job and delivering our own service with other agencies alongside. Both look the same in the data.
41	- There is no rule for when an incident type should be updated, so update practice varies with each individual's experience and view of what should happen. When a rescue becomes a drowning, the type is frequently overwritten and the rescue is lost from the record. Major Rescues cannot be reliably searched, because some are no longer typed as rescues.
42	- The same confusion exists between records. There is no clear rule for when something is an incident, a rescue log, or a first aid form, so it is done inconsistently, and our statistics inherit that inconsistency.
43	
44	These problems share a single root cause. No field in the current model carries a written definition, so practice on each has drifted into individual interpretation.
45	
46	**The cost.** Every season, the EMCaR team pulls incident data for SLSA, for councils, for LSV, and for our own clubs and services. Because the data cannot be taken at face value, each pull requires manual interrogation and correction before the figures can be relied upon. The effort is substantial, it recurs every season, and it limits what can be delivered, leaving reporting that cannot be produced, trends that cannot be seen, and questions that cannot be answered.
47	
48	## Why now
49	
50	The need to redesign incident categorisation has been recognised for years. It has not been done because the problem is complex. There are 72 types, years of accumulated practice, and various dependencies. The underlying solution, whilst detailed, is simple, and every element of the design follows from a single principle set out in Part 2.
51	
52	Two developments make this the right time.
53	
54	**The role has changed.** LSV Comms once spent much of its effort signing on every unit. Digital advances in LIMSOC have removed that workload. The principal responsibility of LSV Comms is now data quality, capturing what happened in an incident accurately and consistently. This proposal is a direct exercise of that responsibility.
55	
56	**The approach is proven.** Last season the first aid form was rebuilt from a rudimentary form that was not fit for purpose. The previous form asked a small set of fixed questions that frequently did not match the situation and gave members no way to record the details that mattered. The replacement asks questions based on what occurred. Where oxygen use is recorded, the oxygen questions are presented. The result was visibility that had not existed before. For the first time the data could be interrogated with confidence, showing which first aid presentations are trending, where forms are completed incorrectly, and what is occurring on our beaches. This proposal applies the same transformation to the incident record.
57	
58	The risk profile of the change should also be stated clearly. The current structure is already producing inconsistent data, and every season it operates adds to that inconsistency. The transition carries effort, but it carries no realistic risk of degrading data quality below its current state. It can only improve it.
59	
60	---
61	
62	# Part 2. The proposal
63	
64	## One idea
65	
66	The model rests on one principle. Every value attached to an incident answers exactly one question, and no two mechanisms answer the same question. This removes ambiguity, streamlines the workflow for members, and eliminates the duplication that degrades data quality today. The result is a simpler model that is easier to use and produces better data.
67	
68	Each mechanism is given a written definition, for the first time:
69	
70	| Question | Mechanism | Cardinality | Example |
71	|----------|-----------|-------------|---------|
72	| What is it, fundamentally | Type (inheritance tree) | one | SAR, Rescue, Person |
73	| What qualifies or characterises it | Tags (the Incident Labels work, priority 1.8) | many | Resuscitation, Rescue Completed, External Request |
74	| Where is it in the lifecycle | Agency Status | one at a time | Responding, On Scene, Under Control |
75	| How did it end | Incident Outcome | one, gated by Type | Resolved, False Alarm, Fatality, Located |
76	| Assistance provided to one individual | Action Log (proposed merge of first aid form and rescue log, see below) | one per person helped | rescue, resus, fracture, marine sting |
77	| Part of a bigger event | Event | one | Wye River Floods |
78	| Free-form situational context | Incident Log | append-only | narrative entries with author and time |
79	| Free-form summary | Incident Name and Incident Brief | one each | short human-readable identifiers |
80	
81	**Governing rule.** A value only earns its place as a Type if it changes what the incident fundamentally is. Otherwise it is a Tag, a Status, an Outcome, or Action Log detail.
82	
83	Two definitions anchor everything else:
84	
85	**Incident.** A response by Life Saving Victoria members that either:
86	
87	- Requires a response from multiple lifesaving services, or
88	- Requires assistance from other emergency services, including all situations where there is a danger to human life, or
89	- Is otherwise serious or complex such that members would like support, assistance, and visibility from LSV Command.
90

- **Guided questions get smarter over time.** Centrally governed question flows can grow per Type without adding types or fields.

- **Member expectations can be raised.** With clear definitions and a simpler workflow, more can be asked of members, because the correct process becomes the easiest process to follow.

📃 CONTENT:

**v0.8.3 is in the Outbox** (46.7 KB, 21:01) and supersedes everything prior: `00_Outbox/LIMSOC Incident Categorisation - Operational Change Proposal Pack v0.8.3.docx`.

**Your edits, checked and applied.** The diff against my last export found exactly one content edit from you, the "Why now" paragraph. I carried it into the source with one cleanup: your deletion left a stray "complex:." which now reads "...because the problem is complex. There are 72 types, years of accumulated practice, and various dependencies. The underlying solution, whilst detailed, is simple..." Everything else in the diff was Word table-reflow noise, so nothing else of yours was touched or lost.

**The colon sweep.** All intra-sentence colons are gone from prose, rewritten as separate sentences or connected clauses (about 20 instances, including "data quality: capturing" → "data quality, capturing", "both facts are preserved: the incident was" → two sentences, and the Rule 2 supporting-principles run-on which became a proper three-bullet list). Heading colons went too: "Part 1: The case for change" is now "Part 1. The case for change", same for Rules 1 to 4 and Annexes A to D, and the "One idea" heading dropped its subtitle (which duplicated its own first sentence). Semicolons were swept in the same pass, all seven of them. What I deliberately kept: colons that introduce a bulleted list or table (seven of those, standard documentation form), and the `Type:` / `Tag:` notation in the migration map, which the Annex A legend defines. Tell me if you want those gone as well.

**Expressive language.** "Genuinely complex" was yours to kill and "genuinely co-occur" went with it. I also scanned for remaining intensifiers: "substantial" (the EMCaR effort) and "rudimentary" (the old first aid form) survive because they carry factual weight, and "industry-leading" stays because you directed it. Final greps confirm zero prose colons, zero semicolons, zero em dashes, zero "genuinely".

One process note: the first v0.8.3 upload went out before my verification grep ran and contained the seven semicolon stragglers; the copy now in the Outbox (21:01) is the corrected one, so make sure Word shows v0.8.3 opened fresh rather than a cached copy.
